phrases.note: Common in casual conversation, similar to 'I see your point'.

phrases.meaning: A more informal way to offer a tentative or slightly hesitant opinion or description.
phrases.example: I guess you could say I'm happy with the results, but there's room for improvement.
phrases.plain: I suppose I'm happy with the results, but there's room for improvement.
phrases.note: Similar to 'I suppose you could say,' but more common in everyday speech.

phrases.meaning: Used to express a premonition or intuition about something that later proved true.
phrases.example: I had a feeling the meeting would be cancelled, and sure enough, it was.
phrases.plain: I had an intuition the meeting would be cancelled, and it was.
phrases.note: Suggests a sense of foresight or intuition, often used after an event.

phrases.meaning: Expressing a specific doubt or concern about a plan or idea.
phrases.example: I have a reservation about the proposed timeline; it seems very ambitious.
phrases.plain: I have a concern about the proposed timeline; it seems very ambitious.
phrases.note: Often followed by "about" and then the specific point of concern.

phrases.meaning: Introduce a piece of advice or an alternative idea in a polite way.
phrases.example: I have a suggestion regarding the report's structure that might make it clearer for readers.
phrases.plain: I want to suggest something about the report's structure to make it clearer.
phrases.note: A polite and common way to offer advice without sounding demanding.

phrases.meaning: Expressing uncertainty or skepticism about something.
phrases.example: I have my doubts about whether that strategy will be effective in the long run.
phrases.plain: I'm skeptical about whether that strategy will be effective in the long run.
phrases.note: A polite way to express reservations without directly saying "you are wrong".

phrases.meaning: Introduces a strong opinion or observation, often one that is important or surprising.
phrases.example: I have to say, your presentation was incredibly clear and persuasive.
phrases.plain: I must state, your presentation was incredibly clear and persuasive.
phrases.note: A common way to introduce a strong, often positive, personal observation or opinion.

phrases.meaning: Acknowledging someone's statement before expressing a different view.
phrases.example: I hear what you're saying about the workload, but this project is a priority.
phrases.plain: I understand your point about the workload, but this project is a priority.
phrases.note: Often followed by "but" or "however" to introduce a counter-argument.

phrases.text: I hope that answers your question
phrases.form: I hope that answers your question
phrases.meaning: Used to politely conclude your response and check if the questioner is satisfied.
phrases.example: I've explained the process in detail, so I hope that answers your question.
phrases.plain: I've explained the process in detail, so I hope you are satisfied with the answer.
phrases.note: A polite closing to a Q&A interaction. Professional and considerate.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission or to soften a potentially intrusive action.
phrases.example: I hope you don't mind, but I've already ordered coffee for everyone.
phrases.plain: I hope you are okay with this, but I've already ordered coffee for everyone.
phrases.note: Used to check if an action is acceptable, often when it's already been done or is about to be.

phrases.text: I hope you found this useful
phrases.form: I hope you found this useful
phrases.meaning: Used to express a wish that the audience gained value from your presentation.
phrases.example: I hope you found this useful for your upcoming project.
phrases.plain: I hope this was helpful for your upcoming project.
phrases.note: A polite and common way to end a presentation, inviting positive feedback.

phrases.meaning: Introduce the purpose of your communication, often to give feedback or make a point.
phrases.example: I just wanted to mention that the report contains a few minor typos.
phrases.plain: I wanted to mention that the report contains a few minor typos.
phrases.note: A common, informal way to introduce a point, often a gentle one.

phrases.text: I just wanted to check in
phrases.form: I just wanted to check in
phrases.meaning: Initiate a conversation to see how someone is doing or to get an update.
phrases.example: I just wanted to check in on your progress with the new software implementation.
phrases.plain: I wanted to ask about your progress with the new software implementation.
phrases.note: A common, informal way to start a conversation, often for a quick update or to offer support.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a brief, often important, point or clarification.
phrases.example: Before we move on, I just wanted to say that I agree with your assessment.
phrases.plain: Before we move on, I want to state that I agree with your assessment.
phrases.note: A common, slightly informal way to add a quick thought or opinion.

phrases.meaning: Expresses empathy by indicating shared experience or understanding of emotions.
phrases.example: When my laptop crashed last week, I know how you feel about losing all that unsaved work.
phrases.plain: When my laptop crashed last week, I understand your frustration about losing all that unsaved work.
phrases.note: Can be comforting, but ensure you genuinely relate to avoid sounding dismissive.

phrases.meaning: Used to clarify or rephrase a previous statement, or to emphasize a point.
phrases.example: It's not ideal, I mean to say, we could do much better with more resources.
phrases.plain: It's not ideal; I want to clarify that we could do much better with more resources.
phrases.note: A common filler phrase used to elaborate or correct oneself.

phrases.meaning: Used to admit that you said something incorrectly or unintentionally.
phrases.example: I misspoke earlier; the project launch is in Q3, not Q2.
phrases.plain: I said something incorrectly earlier; the project launch is in Q3, not Q2.
phrases.note: A direct and professional way to acknowledge a verbal error. Common.

phrases.meaning: Introduces an acknowledgement or confession, often of something slightly unexpected or reluctant.
phrases.example: I must admit, I was skeptical at first, but the new system is actually quite efficient.
phrases.plain: I confess, I was skeptical at first, but the new system is actually quite efficient.
phrases.note: Used to introduce a concession or a slightly surprising personal admission.

phrases.meaning: to state that you require help with a specific task.
phrases.example: I need assistance with checking in my oversized baggage.
phrases.plain: I require help with checking in my oversized baggage.
phrases.note: Slightly more formal than 'could you help me'.

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say you need to leave the call or meeting.
phrases.example: Apologies, but I need to jump off for another meeting in five minutes.
phrases.plain: Apologies, but I need to leave this call for another meeting in five minutes.
phrases.note: Informal and common, especially in video calls, to politely excuse oneself.

phrases.meaning: To express sincere gratitude for something.
phrases.example: Thanks for picking me up from the airport, I really appreciate it.
phrases.plain: Thanks for picking me up from the airport, I am very grateful.
phrases.note: Versatile for expressing thanks for a favour or kindness.

phrases.meaning: Used to share a specific thought or internal reaction from a past moment.
phrases.example: I remember thinking, 'This is going to be a disaster,' right before it started.
phrases.plain: I thought, 'This is going to be a disaster,' right before it started.
phrases.note: Adds a personal, reflective layer to storytelling, revealing inner thoughts.

phrases.meaning: Stating that you have a different perspective or opinion.
phrases.example: I see things differently when it comes to the best way to handle client feedback.
phrases.plain: My opinion is different regarding the best way to handle client feedback.
phrases.note: A gentle and non-confrontational way to introduce an alternative viewpoint.

phrases.meaning: Indicate that you understand someone's perspective or explanation.
phrases.example: I see what you mean about the client's expectations; they are quite high for this project.
phrases.plain: I understand your point about the client's expectations; they are quite high.
phrases.note: A common, neutral phrase to show understanding.

phrases.meaning: Acknowledging the validity of someone else's argument or perspective.
phrases.example: I see your point about the budget constraints, but we still need to invest in quality.
phrases.plain: I understand your argument about the budget, but we still need to invest in quality.
phrases.note: A common way to acknowledge another's view before presenting a counter-argument.

phrases.meaning: to indicate that you are about to provide a necessary explanation.
phrases.example: Before we proceed, I should explain the new safety protocols in detail.
phrases.plain: Before we proceed, I will explain the new safety protocols in detail.
phrases.note: Polite and formal way to introduce an explanation.

phrases.meaning: Expresses reluctant or hesitant agreement, often implying a lack of strong conviction.
phrases.example: Should we just reschedule for next week? I suppose so, there's no other option.
phrases.plain: Should we just reschedule for next week? I guess so, there's no other option.
phrases.note: A common way to agree without much enthusiasm or when there's no better alternative.

phrases.meaning: Used to offer a tentative or slightly hesitant opinion or description.
phrases.example: I suppose you could say the meeting was productive, though we didn't decide much.
phrases.plain: You could perhaps say the meeting was productive, though we didn't decide much.
phrases.note: Suggests a cautious or qualified agreement, or a less definitive statement.

phrases.meaning: Accept complete blame or accountability for a mistake or outcome.
phrases.example: I take full responsibility for the oversight in the budget calculations; it won't happen again.
phrases.plain: I am completely responsible for the oversight in the budget calculations; it won't happen again.
phrases.note: A strong and direct way to admit fault.

phrases.meaning: Acknowledging someone's argument, often before disagreeing.
phrases.example: I take your point about the tight deadline, but we have to deliver on time.
phrases.plain: I understand your argument about the tight deadline, but we have to deliver on time.
phrases.note: Similar to "I see your point," but can imply a slightly more active consideration.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you have grasped the meaning, possibly with a slight reservation.
phrases.example: Okay, I think I understand your perspective on the budget constraints.
phrases.plain: Okay, I understand your perspective on the budget constraints.
phrases.note: A cautious way to confirm understanding, leaving room for further clarification.

phrases.meaning: A statement indicating that you have finished your contribution or the discussion is complete.
phrases.example: From my side, I think that's all for today's update.
phrases.plain: From my side, I believe my update is complete for today.
phrases.note: Informal and common way to signal the end of one's turn or the meeting.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that another participant has disconnected from the call.
phrases.example: I think we lost Sarah; she's no longer showing in the participant list.
phrases.plain: I think Sarah disconnected; she's no longer showing in the participant list.
phrases.note: A polite way to acknowledge a participant's unexpected departure from a call.

phrases.meaning: Introduce a suggestion or recommendation for a course of action.
phrases.example: I think we should schedule a follow-up meeting to discuss these points further.
phrases.plain: We should schedule a follow-up meeting to discuss these points further.
phrases.note: A direct but collaborative way to suggest an action.

phrases.text: I think we're out of time
phrases.form: I think we're out of time
phrases.meaning: A polite way to indicate that the allotted time for the discussion has expired.
phrases.example: Unfortunately, I think we're out of time for further discussion on this point.
phrases.plain: Unfortunately, our time has expired for further discussion on this point.
phrases.note: Common and polite way to manage meeting time, often used by a facilitator.

phrases.meaning: Expresses complete and enthusiastic agreement with someone's statement.
phrases.example: I totally agree that we need to prioritize employee well-being in this company.
phrases.plain: I completely agree that we need to prioritize employee well-being in this company.
phrases.note: A common, informal way to express strong agreement.

phrases.meaning: Acknowledge someone's worry or issue, showing empathy.
phrases.example: I understand your concern about the project's scope, and we're actively managing it.
phrases.plain: I recognize your worry about the project's scope, and we're actively managing it.
phrases.note: A polite and empathetic way to respond to someone's worry.

phrases.meaning: Used to strongly emphasize a particular point or statement.
phrases.example: I want to stress that collaboration is essential for this project's success.
phrases.plain: Collaboration is essential for this project's success.
phrases.note: A direct and forceful way to highlight importance. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a question about a specific topic.
phrases.example: Before we move on, I wanted to ask about the next steps for the project.
phrases.plain: Before we move on, I had a question about the next steps for the project.
phrases.note: Common way to introduce a question, often after someone else has spoken.

phrases.meaning: Introduce a topic briefly or mention it as part of a broader discussion.
phrases.example: I wanted to touch on your performance this quarter, specifically your excellent client communication.
phrases.plain: I wanted to briefly mention your performance this quarter, specifically your excellent client communication.
phrases.note: A polite way to introduce a topic, often implying it's one of several points.

phrases.meaning: Expresses a past expectation or desire that was not met, implying disappointment.
phrases.example: I was hoping for a quick resolution to the issue, but it seems it will take longer.
phrases.plain: I expected a quick resolution to the issue, but it seems it will take longer.
phrases.note: A polite way to express disappointment by stating a previous, unfulfilled hope.

phrases.text: I was just thinking about you
phrases.form: I was just thinking about you
phrases.meaning: A friendly expression used when you encounter someone you were recently considering.
phrases.example: Oh, hi! I was just thinking about you and that project.
phrases.plain: Oh, hi! I was recently considering you and that project.
phrases.note: Creates an immediate connection and makes the other person feel acknowledged.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to introduce a question or a tentative suggestion.
phrases.example: I was just wondering if you'd heard anything about the new project.
phrases.plain: I wanted to ask if you'd heard anything about the new project.
phrases.note: Softens a question, making it less direct. Useful for gentle inquiries.

phrases.meaning: Used to express being surprised or shocked, often in a negative way.
phrases.example: I was taken aback by his sudden outburst during the presentation.
phrases.plain: I was surprised by his sudden outburst during the presentation.
phrases.note: Indicates a moment of shock or surprise that causes a pause or hesitation.

phrases.meaning: To introduce a suggestion or idea for an activity.
phrases.example: I was thinking of having a small get-together at my place on Friday.
phrases.plain: I had the idea of having a small get-together at my place on Friday.
phrases.note: Polite and common way to propose an activity or plan.

phrases.meaning: A polite and indirect way to ask a question or make a request.
phrases.example: I was wondering if you'd be free for a quick chat later.
phrases.plain: Would you be free for a quick chat later?
phrases.note: Very polite and less demanding than a direct question. Useful for requests.

phrases.meaning: Offer advice or a recommendation in a polite and indirect manner.
phrases.example: I would suggest that we revisit the budget figures before presenting them to the board.
phrases.plain: I recommend that we revisit the budget figures before presenting them to the board.
phrases.note: A polite and professional way to give advice.

phrases.meaning: Expresses polite disagreement or a gentle correction of someone's statement.
phrases.example: You think the new policy is a complete disaster? I wouldn't say that, it has some benefits.
phrases.plain: You think the new policy is a complete disaster? I disagree, it has some benefits.
phrases.note: A diplomatic way to express disagreement without being confrontational.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a point that you believe strongly in and are prepared to defend.
phrases.example: I'd argue that our current strategy isn't sustainable in the long run.
phrases.plain: I believe strongly that our current strategy isn't sustainable in the long run.
phrases.note: A confident way to present a debatable point.

phrases.meaning: Used to politely offer to provide a response to a question.
phrases.example: That's a great point, and I'd be happy to answer that for you.
phrases.plain: That's a great point, and I can answer that for you.
phrases.note: A polite and welcoming way to respond to a question. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Expressing reluctance or caution about taking a particular action.
phrases.example: I'd be hesitant to approve the budget without a detailed breakdown of expenses.
phrases.plain: I'd be reluctant to approve the budget without a detailed breakdown of expenses.
phrases.note: Indicates a strong reservation before committing to something.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to express your desire to listen to someone's opinion or information.
phrases.example: I'd be interested to hear about the company's approach to diversity and inclusion.
phrases.plain: I'd like to hear about the company's approach to diversity and inclusion.
phrases.note: Shows engagement and active listening. Very professional for asking questions.

phrases.meaning: Suggest or advise someone to take a particular action.
phrases.example: I'd encourage you to seek out more training opportunities in project management.
phrases.plain: I advise you to seek out more training opportunities in project management.
phrases.note: A polite and supportive way to give advice or suggest development.

phrases.meaning: A polite but firm way to state your disagreement.
phrases.example: I'd have to disagree with the assessment that the project is ahead of schedule.
phrases.plain: I disagree with the assessment that the project is ahead of schedule.
phrases.note: The "have to" adds a sense of obligation, making it sound less personal.

phrases.meaning: Introduce an additional point or piece of information to a discussion.
phrases.example: I'd like to add that the team's collaboration on this project was exceptional.
phrases.plain: I want to also say that the team's collaboration on this project was exceptional.
phrases.note: A polite way to contribute an extra point to a conversation.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce the starting point or initial focus of your talk.
phrases.example: I'd like to begin by thanking you all for coming today.
phrases.plain: I want to start by thanking everyone for attending today.
phrases.note: A polite and standard opening for a presentation. Slightly formal but widely used.

phrases.meaning: to express a desire to make something clearer or more precise.
phrases.example: I'd like to clarify my previous statement about the budget allocation.
phrases.plain: I want to make my previous statement about the budget allocation clearer.
phrases.note: Polite and formal way to offer clarification.

phrases.meaning: to express dissatisfaction with a service or product.
phrases.example: I'd like to complain about the noise from the room next door.
phrases.plain: I want to express my dissatisfaction with the noise from the room next door.
phrases.note: Polite but firm way to make a complaint.

phrases.meaning: Used to signal the end of your presentation and introduce your final statement.
phrases.example: I'd like to conclude by thanking you all for your valuable time.
phrases.plain: I want to finish by thanking you all for your valuable time.
phrases.note: A polite and standard closing for a presentation. Very professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to verify information or an agreement.
phrases.example: I'd like to confirm the action points before we close the meeting.
phrases.plain: I want to verify the action points before we close the meeting.
phrases.note: Professional way to ensure accuracy and agreement. Neutral register.

phrases.text: I'd like to draw your attention to
phrases.form: I'd like to draw your attention to
phrases.meaning: Used to politely ask the audience to focus on a specific detail or point.
phrases.example: I'd like to draw your attention to the third bullet point on the slide.
phrases.plain: Please look at the third bullet point on the slide.
phrases.note: A formal and polite way to highlight something important. Very professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to highlight a particular point as being very important.
phrases.example: I'd like to emphasize the importance of clear communication within the team.
phrases.plain: I want to highlight the importance of clear communication within the team.
phrases.note: A formal and direct way to stress a point. Professional.

phrases.text: I'd like to get your feedback
phrases.form: I'd like to get your feedback
phrases.meaning: Used to ask someone for their opinion or reaction to something.
phrases.example: I'd like to get your feedback on the draft proposal by end of day.
phrases.plain: I want to get your opinion on the draft proposal by end of day.
phrases.note: Polite way to solicit constructive criticism or input. Collaborative.

phrases.text: I'd like to get your input
phrases.form: I'd like to get your input
phrases.meaning: Used to ask someone for their opinion, ideas, or feedback.
phrases.example: Before we finalize, I'd like to get your input on the design changes.
phrases.plain: Before we finalize, I want to get your opinion on the design changes.
phrases.note: Polite way to solicit feedback. Encourages collaboration.

phrases.text: I'd like to get your perspective
phrases.form: I'd like to get your perspective
phrases.meaning: Used to ask someone for their viewpoint or way of looking at a situation.
phrases.example: I'd like to get your perspective on the challenges we're facing.
phrases.plain: I want to get your viewpoint on the challenges we're facing.
phrases.note: Polite way to solicit input. Encourages diverse opinions.

phrases.text: I'd like to get your thoughts on
phrases.form: I'd like to get your thoughts on
phrases.meaning: Used to invite someone to share their opinions or ideas about a topic.
phrases.example: I'd like to get your thoughts on the new marketing strategy, Maria.
phrases.plain: I want to hear your opinions on the new marketing strategy, Maria.
phrases.note: Polite way to solicit input. Encourages participation.

phrases.text: I'd like to get your thoughts on this
phrases.form: I'd like to get your thoughts on this
phrases.meaning: Used to invite someone to share their opinions or ideas about a specific topic.
phrases.example: Before we finalize, I'd like to get your thoughts on this new proposal.
phrases.plain: Before we finalize, I want to hear your opinions on this new proposal.
phrases.note: Polite way to solicit input. Encourages participation.

phrases.meaning: Used to invite a specific person to share their thoughts or input.
phrases.example: Now, I'd like to hear from Sarah regarding the marketing campaign.
phrases.plain: Now, I want to hear Sarah's thoughts regarding the marketing campaign.
phrases.note: Encourages participation from specific individuals. Inclusive.

phrases.text: I'd like to hear your thoughts
phrases.form: I'd like to hear your thoughts
phrases.meaning: Used to invite someone to share their opinions or ideas.
phrases.example: Before we decide, I'd like to hear your thoughts on this proposal.
phrases.plain: Before we decide, I want to hear your opinions on this proposal.
phrases.note: Polite way to solicit input. Encourages participation.

phrases.meaning: A formal way to express a desire to interrupt and add a comment or question.
phrases.example: If I may, I'd like to interject a quick question about the project timeline.
phrases.plain: If I may, I want to add a quick question about the project timeline.
phrases.note: More formal than "jump in," suitable for professional settings.

phrases.text: I'd like to make a comment
phrases.form: I'd like to make a comment
phrases.meaning: Used to offer a remark or observation on a topic.
phrases.example: If I may, I'd like to make a comment on the proposed changes.
phrases.plain: If I may, I want to offer a remark on the proposed changes.
phrases.note: Polite way to contribute to the discussion. Neutral register.

phrases.text: I'd like to make a point
phrases.form: I'd like to make a point
phrases.meaning: Used to introduce an important idea or argument for consideration.
phrases.example: Before we conclude, I'd like to make a point about resource allocation.
phrases.plain: Before we conclude, I want to mention something important about resources.
phrases.note: Polite and common way to introduce a new topic or concern. Neutral register.

phrases.text: I'd like to make a suggestion
phrases.form: I'd like to make a suggestion
phrases.meaning: Used to offer an idea or recommendation for consideration.
phrases.example: I'd like to make a suggestion regarding the team's workflow.
phrases.plain: I want to offer an idea regarding the team's workflow.
phrases.note: Polite and common way to introduce a suggestion. Neutral register.

phrases.meaning: Used to suggest transitioning to the next topic or stage of discussion.
phrases.example: If there are no further comments, I'd like to move on to the next item.
phrases.plain: If there are no further comments, I want to go to the next item.
phrases.note: Polite way to steer the meeting forward. Often used by the chair.

phrases.meaning: Introducing an alternative idea or perspective for consideration.
phrases.example: I'd like to offer a different perspective on how we approach this challenge.
phrases.plain: I want to present a different perspective on how we approach this challenge.
phrases.note: A polite way to introduce a new idea or counter-argument.

phrases.text: I'd like to open the floor
phrases.form: I'd like to open the floor
phrases.meaning: To invite participants to ask questions or offer comments.
phrases.example: Now, I'd like to open the floor for any questions or additional comments.
phrases.plain: Now, I want to invite questions or additional comments from everyone.
phrases.note: Formal way to invite general discussion. Used by the meeting leader.

phrases.meaning: Used to draw attention to a specific fact or detail.
phrases.example: I'd like to point out that our budget is quite limited this quarter.
phrases.plain: I want to mention that our budget is quite limited this quarter.
phrases.note: Highlights an important piece of information. Can be used to raise a concern.

phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest an idea or course of action.
phrases.example: I'd like to propose that we allocate more resources to the marketing team.
phrases.plain: I want to suggest that we allocate more resources to the marketing team.
phrases.note: Formal and direct way to make a suggestion. Professional context.

phrases.text: I'd like to propose a budget
phrases.form: I'd like to propose a budget
phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest a financial plan or allocation of funds.
phrases.example: Based on our needs, I'd like to propose a budget of 50,000 for this project.
phrases.plain: Based on our needs, I want to suggest a budget of 50,000 for this project.
phrases.note: Professional way to introduce a financial plan. Planning-oriented.

phrases.text: I'd like to propose a meeting
phrases.form: I'd like to propose a meeting
phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest scheduling a discussion or gathering.
phrases.example: To address these issues, I'd like to propose a meeting next week.
phrases.plain: To address these issues, I want to suggest a meeting next week.
phrases.note: Professional way to initiate further discussion. Action-oriented.

phrases.text: I'd like to propose a new idea
phrases.form: I'd like to propose a new idea
phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest a novel concept or plan.
phrases.example: I'd like to propose a new idea for our next marketing campaign.
phrases.plain: I want to suggest a new idea for our next marketing campaign.
phrases.note: Direct and professional way to introduce innovation. Creative.

phrases.text: I'd like to propose a solution
phrases.form: I'd like to propose a solution
phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest a way to resolve a problem or issue.
phrases.example: To address this, I'd like to propose a solution involving new software.
phrases.plain: To address this, I want to suggest a solution involving new software.
phrases.note: Direct and professional way to offer a resolution. Solution-oriented.

phrases.text: I'd like to propose a timeline
phrases.form: I'd like to propose a timeline
phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest a schedule or sequence of events.
phrases.example: To ensure efficiency, I'd like to propose a timeline for the next phase.
phrases.plain: To ensure efficiency, I want to suggest a schedule for the next phase.
phrases.note: Professional way to introduce a project schedule. Planning-oriented.

phrases.text: I'd like to propose a vote
phrases.form: I'd like to propose a vote
phrases.meaning: Used to formally suggest that a decision be made by voting.
phrases.example: Since we have differing opinions, I'd like to propose a vote on the matter.
phrases.plain: Since we have differing opinions, I want to suggest we vote on the matter.
phrases.note: Formal way to move towards a decision when consensus is difficult.

phrases.meaning: Politely expressing disagreement or resistance to a proposal or idea.
phrases.example: I'd like to push back on the idea of cutting the training budget this year.
phrases.plain: I want to disagree with the idea of cutting the training budget this year.
phrases.note: Common in professional contexts, indicating a desire to challenge a decision or statement.

phrases.meaning: Introduce a topic for discussion, often a concern or a point that needs attention.
phrases.example: I'd like to raise a point about the budget allocation for the upcoming marketing campaign.
phrases.plain: I want to discuss the budget allocation for the upcoming marketing campaign.
phrases.note: A polite and professional way to introduce a topic, often a concern.

phrases.text: I'd like to raise a point
phrases.form: I'd like to raise a point
phrases.meaning: To introduce an idea or question for discussion.
phrases.example: Before we move on, I'd like to raise a point about the budget allocation.
phrases.plain: Before we move on, I'd like to mention something about the budget.
phrases.note: Polite and common way to introduce a new topic or concern. Neutral register.

phrases.meaning: Used to repeat or emphasize a point for clarity or importance.
phrases.example: I'd like to reiterate the importance of meeting these deadlines.
phrases.plain: I want to repeat the importance of meeting these deadlines.
phrases.note: Formal way to stress a point. Used when a message needs reinforcement.

phrases.meaning: Express a desire for a particular action or outcome, often as a suggestion.
phrases.example: I'd like to see more proactive communication from the team on potential roadblocks.
phrases.plain: I want to see more proactive communication from the team on potential roadblocks.
phrases.note: A common way for a manager to express expectations or desired changes.

phrases.meaning: Used to offer an idea or recommendation for consideration.
phrases.example: I'd like to suggest we explore alternative solutions before committing.
phrases.plain: I want to suggest we explore alternative solutions before committing.
phrases.note: Polite and common way to introduce a suggestion. Neutral register.

phrases.text: I'd like to suggest a break
phrases.form: I'd like to suggest a break
phrases.meaning: Used to propose taking a short pause during a meeting.
phrases.example: We've been discussing for an hour, so I'd like to suggest a break.
phrases.plain: We've been discussing for an hour, so I want to suggest a break.
phrases.note: Polite way to propose a pause. Considers participant fatigue.

phrases.text: I'd like to suggest an alternative
phrases.form: I'd like to suggest an alternative
phrases.meaning: Used to offer a different idea or course of action.
phrases.example: I'd like to suggest an alternative approach to solving this problem.
phrases.plain: I want to suggest a different way to solve this problem.
phrases.note: Polite way to introduce a new option. Constructive and problem-solving.

phrases.meaning: Used to offer an idea or recommendation for consideration.
phrases.example: I'd like to suggest that we postpone the decision until next week.
phrases.plain: I want to suggest that we postpone the decision until next week.
phrases.note: Polite and common way to introduce a suggestion. Neutral register.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to decline an invitation while expressing a desire to accept.
phrases.example: I'd love to but I already have plans that night.
phrases.plain: I would really like to come but I already have plans that night.
phrases.note: Standard polite refusal, softening the rejection.

phrases.meaning: Offer a strong suggestion or piece of advice.
phrases.example: I'd recommend that you review the client's previous feedback before finalizing the design.
phrases.plain: I advise you to review the client's previous feedback before finalizing the design.
phrases.note: A professional way to give advice, slightly stronger than "I would suggest".

phrases.meaning: A promise to re-establish communication after a period of silence.
phrases.example: I'll review your proposal and I'll be back in touch by the end of the week.
phrases.plain: I'll review your proposal and I will contact you again by the end of the week.
phrases.note: Common closing, implying a future follow-up after a task is completed.

phrases.meaning: A promise to contact the other person again in the near future.
phrases.example: Thanks for the update; I'll be in touch next week with our decision.
phrases.plain: Thanks for the update; I will contact you next week with our decision.
phrases.note: Common closing, indicating future communication, can be formal or informal.

phrases.meaning: A promise to contact someone very soon.
phrases.example: Thanks for your inquiry; I'll be in touch shortly with a response.
phrases.plain: Thanks for your inquiry; I will contact you very soon with a response.
phrases.note: Polite and professional way to indicate a quick follow-up.

phrases.meaning: A promise to contact the other person in the near future.
phrases.example: I'll review the documents and I'll be in touch soon with my feedback.
phrases.plain: I'll review the documents and I will contact you soon with my feedback.
phrases.note: Common and polite closing, indicating future communication without a specific date.

phrases.meaning: States that you will not be at your workplace and likely unavailable.
phrases.example: I'll be out of office next week, so please contact my colleague.
phrases.plain: I will not be at my workplace next week, so please contact my colleague.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for automatic email replies or informing colleagues.

phrases.meaning: Promise to definitely take a specific action.
phrases.example: I'll be sure to include your feedback in the revised project proposal.
phrases.plain: I will definitely include your feedback in the revised project proposal.
phrases.note: A strong commitment to perform an action.

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say "I'll see you later" or "I'll talk to you later."
phrases.example: I need to grab another drink, I'll catch you later!
phrases.plain: I need to grab another drink, I will see you again later!
phrases.note: Very informal, used when temporarily parting ways at an event.

phrases.meaning: To promise to provide a definite answer at a subsequent time.
phrases.example: I'm not sure about Saturday yet, I'll confirm later tonight.
phrases.plain: I'm not sure about Saturday yet, I will give a definite answer later tonight.
phrases.note: Useful when you need time to finalize plans.

phrases.meaning: Promise to try as hard as possible to achieve something.
phrases.example: I'll do my best to incorporate your feedback into the next iteration of the design.
phrases.plain: I will try my hardest to incorporate your feedback into the next iteration of the design.
phrases.note: A common, reassuring phrase when committing to an effort.

phrases.meaning: An informal promise to send a short message, usually an email or text.
phrases.example: I'll drop you a line later today with the meeting agenda.
phrases.plain: I will send you a short message later today with the meeting agenda.
phrases.note: Informal and friendly way to say you'll send a message.

phrases.meaning: An informal promise to send an email.
phrases.example: I'll confirm the details and then I'll drop you an email with the summary.
phrases.plain: I'll confirm the details and then I will send you an email with the summary.
phrases.note: Informal and friendly way to say you'll send an email.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to check the status or progress of a specific item.
phrases.example: I'll follow up on that request with the team and let you know.
phrases.plain: I will check the status of that request with the team and let you know.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings for tracking tasks or information.

phrases.meaning: Promise to take further action or investigate a matter.
phrases.example: You raised a question about the client's budget; I'll follow up on that and get back to you.
phrases.plain: You raised a question about the client's budget; I will investigate it and respond.
phrases.note: A common, professional way to commit to taking action on an issue.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to contact someone again later regarding a specific matter.
phrases.example: I'll follow up with an email summarizing our discussion and action points.
phrases.plain: I will send a follow-up email summarizing our discussion and action points.
phrases.note: Very common in professional contexts to confirm next steps or information.

phrases.text: I'll get back to my desk
phrases.form: I'll get back to my desk
phrases.meaning: States an intention to return to one's workspace, often to retrieve information.
phrases.example: I don't have that file here, but I'll get back to my desk and send it to you.
phrases.plain: I don't have that file here, but I will return to my desk and send it to you.
phrases.note: Common phrase when needing to access resources from one's office.

phrases.text: I'll get back to my emails
phrases.form: I'll get back to my emails
phrases.meaning: States an intention to resume checking and responding to emails.
phrases.example: I've finished the call, so I'll get back to my emails now.
phrases.plain: I've finished the call, so I will resume checking and responding to my emails now.
phrases.note: Common phrase to indicate a return to email correspondence after a call.

phrases.meaning: A promise to respond or provide information at a later time.
phrases.example: I don't have that information right now, but I'll get back to you by end of day.
phrases.plain: I don't have that information right now, but I will respond to you by end of day.
phrases.note: Very common phrase for promising a future response, often with a timeframe.

phrases.text: I'll get back to you on
phrases.form: I'll get back to you on
phrases.meaning: A promise to provide a response or information about a specific topic later.
phrases.example: I don't have the figures now, but I'll get back to you on the budget details.
phrases.plain: I don't have the figures now, but I will provide you with the budget details later.
phrases.note: Similar to "I'll get back to you" but specifies the topic.

phrases.meaning: A promise to contact someone, usually by phone or email.
phrases.example: I'll review the proposal and then I'll get in touch with my feedback.
phrases.plain: I'll review the proposal and then I will contact you with my feedback.
phrases.note: Common and versatile phrase for promising future communication.

phrases.meaning: A promise to contact a specific person or department.
phrases.example: I'll get in touch with the sales team regarding your query.
phrases.plain: I will contact the sales team regarding your query.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings when referring a query to another party.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to ensure something is dispatched, usually by email.
phrases.example: Thanks for the information; I'll get that sent to the team right away.
phrases.plain: Thanks for the information; I will ensure it is sent to the team right away.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings for confirming action on a document or email.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to obtain specific data or facts.
phrases.example: I don't have that to hand, but I'll get the information and send it over.
phrases.plain: I don't have that to hand, but I will obtain the information and send it over.
phrases.note: Common in professional contexts when needing to retrieve data.

phrases.meaning: Used to defer answering a question because it will be covered in a subsequent section.
phrases.example: That's an excellent point, and I'll get to that later in my presentation.
phrases.plain: That's an excellent point, and I will discuss that later in my presentation.
phrases.note: A polite way to manage the flow of information without dismissing the question.

phrases.meaning: An informal promise to call someone on the phone.
phrases.example: I'll check my calendar and then I'll give you a ring to confirm our meeting.
phrases.plain: I'll check my calendar and then I will call you to confirm our meeting.
phrases.note: Informal and friendly way to say "I'll call you."

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say "I'll contact you" or "I'll call you."
phrases.example: When I get home, I'll give you a shout to finalize our plans.
phrases.plain: When I get home, I will contact you to finalize our plans.
phrases.note: Very informal, common in British English.

phrases.meaning: Used to formally transfer the speaking turn or responsibility to another person.
phrases.example: Now that I've covered the introduction, I'll hand it over to Mark for the details.
phrases.plain: Now that I've covered the introduction, Mark will speak about the details.
phrases.note: Common in presentations or structured meetings to transition speakers.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to turn off your microphone to avoid background noise.
phrases.example: There's some background noise here, so I'll just mute myself for a moment.
phrases.plain: There's some background noise here, so I will turn off my microphone for a moment.
phrases.note: Polite way to manage audio quality, especially in group calls.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you will cover a series of points rapidly.
phrases.example: I'll just quickly run through the agenda for today's meeting.
phrases.plain: I will quickly go over the agenda for today's meeting.
phrases.note: Suggests efficiency and brevity. Common in informal professional settings.

phrases.meaning: Promise to monitor or pay attention to a situation or issue.
phrases.example: I'll keep an eye on the project's progress to ensure we stay within budget.
phrases.plain: I will monitor the project's progress to ensure we stay within budget.
phrases.note: A common way to reassure someone that you will be vigilant about something.

phrases.meaning: A promise to be concise and not speak for too long.
phrases.example: I know we're short on time, so I'll keep it brief with my update.
phrases.plain: I know we're short on time, so I will be concise with my update.
phrases.note: Polite way to signal that your contribution will be short, respecting others' time.

phrases.meaning: Promise to remember a piece of information or advice for future consideration.
phrases.example: Your suggestion about the new software is helpful; I'll keep that in mind for our next review.
phrases.plain: Your suggestion about the new software is helpful; I'll remember it for our next review.
phrases.note: A common, polite way to acknowledge advice without committing to immediate action.

phrases.meaning: A promise to provide updates as new information becomes available.
phrases.example: I'll let you know about the meeting time. I'll keep you posted.
phrases.plain: I'll let you know about the meeting time. I'll give you updates.
phrases.note: Common and professional. Assures the other person they won't be left out of the loop.

phrases.meaning: A promise to provide new information as it becomes available.
phrases.example: I'll check on that for you and I'll keep you updated on the progress.
phrases.plain: I'll check on that for you and I will inform you of any new progress.
phrases.note: Common in professional and personal contexts for ongoing situations.

phrases.meaning: Indicates that you are finished speaking and the other person can resume their turn.
phrases.example: That's all I wanted to add, so I'll let you continue with your presentation.
phrases.plain: That's all I wanted to add, so please continue with your presentation.
phrases.note: Polite way to hand over the speaking turn after making a point.

phrases.meaning: Indicates that you are giving the other person the opportunity to speak or lead.
phrases.example: I've finished my part, so I'll let you take over the discussion now.
phrases.plain: I've finished my part, so you can lead the discussion now.
phrases.note: Common in meetings to transition leadership or speaking turns.

phrases.meaning: Promise to investigate or examine a matter further.
phrases.example: You mentioned a discrepancy in the figures; I'll look into that right away.
phrases.plain: You mentioned a discrepancy in the figures; I will investigate it right away.
phrases.note: A common, reassuring response when someone raises a problem.

phrases.text: I'll make a note of that
phrases.form: I'll make a note of that
phrases.meaning: Promise to record a piece of information or a suggestion.
phrases.example: That's a good idea for the next meeting agenda; I'll make a note of that.
phrases.plain: That's a good idea for the next meeting agenda; I will write it down.
phrases.note: A common, reassuring phrase indicating that a point has been heard and will be remembered.

phrases.meaning: Promise to take a specific action or ensure something happens.
phrases.example: I'll make sure to double-check all the figures before submitting the final report.
phrases.plain: I will double-check all the figures before submitting the final report.
phrases.note: A common way to reassure someone that you will address their point.

phrases.meaning: Used to emphasize the lasting impact or vivid memory of an event.
phrases.example: I'll never forget the look on his face when he realized his mistake.
phrases.plain: I will always remember the look on his face when he realized his mistake.
phrases.note: Highlights a particularly memorable moment, often emotional or significant.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to temporarily pause the call, usually to find information.
phrases.example: I need to check something, so I'll put you on hold for a minute.
phrases.plain: I need to check something, so I will temporarily pause the call for a minute.
phrases.note: Standard phrase used by customer service or receptionists on phone calls.

phrases.meaning: A promise to contact someone, often in a professional context, by any means.
phrases.example: I'll gather the information and then I'll reach out to you next week.
phrases.plain: I'll gather the information and then I will contact you next week.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings, more formal than "get in touch."

phrases.meaning: A promise to reply to a message or inquiry without delay once a condition is met.
phrases.example: I'll respond as soon as I have all the necessary information from the team.
phrases.plain: I will reply once I have all the necessary information from the team.
phrases.note: Polite and professional way to manage expectations about response time.

phrases.meaning: A polite way for a guest to indicate they can leave without being accompanied.
phrases.example: Don't worry, I'll see myself out, you stay warm inside.
phrases.plain: Don't worry, I can leave by myself, you stay warm inside.
phrases.note: Polite and considerate, used by a guest to avoid inconveniencing the host.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to send an electronic invitation for a meeting.
phrases.example: Let's schedule that for next week; I'll send a calendar invite shortly.
phrases.plain: Let's schedule that for next week; I will send an electronic meeting invitation shortly.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings for formalizing meeting arrangements.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to send a subsequent message or email to reiterate points.
phrases.example: Thanks for the discussion; I'll send a follow-up email with the action points.
phrases.plain: Thanks for the discussion; I will send a subsequent email with the action points.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings to summarize or confirm after a meeting.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to transmit a summary or record of the discussion.
phrases.example: I'll send over the notes from our call by the end of the day.
phrases.plain: I will transmit the notes from our call by the end of the day.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings to ensure everyone has a record of decisions.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to provide current information or progress report.
phrases.example: I'll check the status of your order and I'll send you an update by email.
phrases.plain: I'll check the status of your order and I will email you a progress report.
phrases.note: Common in customer service or project management for providing information.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to transmit a web address or meeting invitation.
phrases.example: I'll send you the link for the video call right before it starts.
phrases.plain: I will transmit the web address for the video call right before it starts.
phrases.note: Common for sharing access to online meetings or resources.

phrases.meaning: Used to signal that you are about to conclude the Q&A session.
phrases.example: We're running short on time, so I'll take one more question.
phrases.plain: We're running short on time, so I will answer one more question.
phrases.note: A clear way to manage time and wrap up the Q&A. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Promise to think about a suggestion or piece of feedback.
phrases.example: Your point about the budget is noted; I'll take that into consideration for the next phase.
phrases.plain: Your point about the budget is noted; I will think about it for the next phase.
phrases.note: A polite way to acknowledge feedback without committing to immediate action.

phrases.meaning: To offer to pay for someone's meal, drink, or activity.
phrases.example: It's your birthday, so I'll treat you to dinner tonight.
phrases.plain: It's your birthday, so I will pay for your dinner tonight.
phrases.note: Friendly and generous offer, common for special occasions or as a thank you.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to leave and rejoin the call to fix a technical issue.
phrases.example: My video is frozen, so I'll try reconnecting to see if that helps.
phrases.plain: My video is frozen, so I will leave and rejoin to see if that helps.
phrases.note: Common solution for persistent audio/video problems on video calls.

phrases.meaning: Promise to make an effort to improve a specific behavior or quality.
phrases.example: I'll try to be more proactive in communicating updates to the team moving forward.
phrases.plain: I will make an effort to communicate updates to the team more proactively.
phrases.note: A common way to respond to constructive criticism by committing to change.

phrases.meaning: A polite offer to accompany a guest to the door when they are leaving.
phrases.example: It's getting late, I'll walk you out to your car.
phrases.plain: It's getting late, I will accompany you to your car.
phrases.note: Hospitable gesture from a host to a departing guest.

phrases.meaning: Promise to address or improve a specific area or task.
phrases.example: You mentioned my presentation style; I'll work on that to make it more engaging.
phrases.plain: You mentioned my presentation style; I will try to improve it.
phrases.note: A common, concise way to accept criticism and commit to improvement.

phrases.meaning: Expressing mild worry or unease about a situation.
phrases.example: I'm a bit concerned about the budget overruns we've seen this quarter.
phrases.plain: I'm slightly worried about the budget overruns this quarter.
phrases.note: A polite and common way to voice a reservation without being overly dramatic.

phrases.meaning: Express a mild worry or reservation about something.
phrases.example: I'm a bit concerned about the tight deadline for this project, given our current workload.
phrases.plain: I'm slightly worried about the tight deadline for this project, given our current workload.
phrases.note: A common and polite way to express a reservation without being overly negative.

phrases.text: I'm a bit fed up with it
phrases.form: I'm a bit fed up with it
phrases.meaning: Expresses mild to moderate annoyance or boredom with a recurring situation.
phrases.example: This constant noise from the construction site, I'm a bit fed up with it now.
phrases.plain: This constant noise from the construction site, I'm quite annoyed by it now.
phrases.note: An informal way to say you've had enough of something annoying.

phrases.meaning: Express a slight concern or apprehension about something.
phrases.example: I'm a little worried about the potential impact of these changes on team morale.
phrases.plain: I'm slightly concerned about the potential impact of these changes on team morale.
phrases.note: A common and polite way to express a mild reservation.

phrases.meaning: Expresses intense excitement and happiness about a personal event or news.
phrases.example: I'm absolutely thrilled that my book was finally published after years of work.
phrases.plain: I'm extremely excited that my book was finally published after years of work.
phrases.note: A strong, emphatic way to convey personal joy and excitement.

phrases.text: I'm afraid I can't make it
phrases.form: I'm afraid I can't make it
phrases.meaning: A polite and common way to decline an invitation.
phrases.example: Thank you for the invitation, but I'm afraid I can't make it to the concert.
phrases.plain: Thank you for the invitation, but I cannot come to the concert.
phrases.note: Standard, polite refusal. Often followed by a brief reason or apology.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to express disagreement, often with a hint of regret.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I disagree with your assessment of the team's performance last quarter.
phrases.plain: I disagree with your assessment of the team's performance last quarter.
phrases.note: The "I'm afraid" softens the directness of the disagreement.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to express disagreement with someone's statement or idea.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I don't agree with your assessment of the market trends.
phrases.plain: I don't agree with your assessment of the market trends.
phrases.note: Softens the disagreement, making it less confrontational. Professional.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to admit you don't understand what someone is saying.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I don't follow your logic on that last point.
phrases.plain: I don't understand your logic on that last point.
phrases.note: Softens the admission of confusion, inviting further explanation. Professional.

phrases.text: I'm afraid I don't have that information
phrases.form: I'm afraid I don't have that information
phrases.meaning: Used to politely state that you do not possess the requested data or knowledge.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I don't have that information readily available right now.
phrases.plain: I don't have that information available right now.
phrases.note: A polite and professional way to admit you don't know something. Avoids guessing.

phrases.text: I'm afraid I have a question
phrases.form: I'm afraid I have a question
phrases.meaning: A polite way to interrupt or introduce a question.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I have a question about the budget figures you just presented.
phrases.plain: I have a question about the budget figures you just presented.
phrases.note: Softens the interruption, making it more polite. Professional.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to express regret when stating something you must do, often leave.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I have to run, I have another meeting starting soon.
phrases.plain: Unfortunately, I must leave, I have another meeting starting soon.
phrases.note: Softens the message, making it sound more apologetic or regretful.

phrases.text: I'm afraid I have to disagree
phrases.form: I'm afraid I have to disagree
phrases.meaning: A polite but firm way to state your opposition to an idea or statement.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I have to disagree with the proposed timeline; it's unrealistic.
phrases.plain: I must disagree with the proposed timeline; it's unrealistic.
phrases.note: More direct than 'I'm not sure about that', but still polite. Professional.

phrases.text: I'm afraid I have to interrupt
phrases.form: I'm afraid I have to interrupt
phrases.meaning: A polite way to break into someone's speech.
phrases.example: I'm afraid I have to interrupt, but we're running short on time.
phrases.plain: I must interrupt, but we're running short on time.
phrases.note: Softens the interruption, making it more polite. Professional.

phrases.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to give a negative answer.
phrases.example: Can you still make it to the workshop tomorrow? I'm afraid not, I have another commitment.
phrases.plain: Can you still make it to the workshop tomorrow? Unfortunately no, I have another commitment.
phrases.note: A common, polite, and slightly apologetic way to say "no."

phrases.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to give an affirmative answer to unwelcome news.
phrases.example: Is the meeting really going to run over time? I'm afraid so, we have a lot to cover.
phrases.plain: Is the meeting really going to run over time? Unfortunately yes, we have a lot to cover.
phrases.note: A common, polite, and slightly apologetic way to say "yes" to something undesirable.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce bad news or an unwelcome piece of information politely.
phrases.example: I'm afraid to say that we've run into some unexpected technical difficulties.
phrases.plain: I regret to inform you that we've run into some unexpected technical difficulties.
phrases.note: A polite and common way to deliver negative news, softening the impact.

phrases.meaning: To indicate that one has everything needed or is ready.
phrases.example: Are you ready to go? Yes, I'm all set.
phrases.plain: Are you ready to go? Yes, I have everything I need.
phrases.note: Versatile, can mean 'I'm ready' or 'I have enough' (e.g., food/drink).

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say one is feeling excited and energetic.
phrases.example: I just got great news, I'm buzzing with excitement!
phrases.plain: I just got great news, I am feeling very excited and energetic!
phrases.note: Informal, often used after good news or a stimulating event.

phrases.meaning: Express strong dedication or promise to a particular goal or action.
phrases.example: I'm committed to improving my time management skills after this feedback session.
phrases.plain: I promise to improve my time management skills after this feedback session.
phrases.note: A strong statement of dedication, often used when accepting criticism.

phrases.meaning: Used to express belief in the ability or success of something or someone.
phrases.example: I'm confident in our team's ability to deliver this project on time.
phrases.plain: I believe strongly in our team's ability to deliver this project on time.
phrases.note: Conveys assurance and trust, often used to inspire confidence in others.

phrases.meaning: Express strong belief or assurance about a future outcome or fact.
phrases.example: I'm confident that with a few adjustments, this proposal will be very strong.
phrases.plain: I strongly believe that with a few adjustments, this proposal will be very strong.
phrases.note: Used to express certainty or positive expectation, often when giving encouraging feedback.

phrases.meaning: Express strong belief in the ability of a group to achieve something.
phrases.example: I'm confident we can overcome these challenges with a collaborative approach.
phrases.plain: I strongly believe we can overcome these challenges with a collaborative approach.
phrases.note: Used to express optimism and encourage teamwork, often after discussing issues.

phrases.meaning: Used to express strong belief or certainty about something.
phrases.example: I'm convinced that investing in employee training will boost productivity significantly.
phrases.plain: I strongly believe that investing in employee training will boost productivity significantly.
phrases.note: Conveys confidence and conviction in your argument.

phrases.meaning: A polite and engaging way to express your interest in learning something.
phrases.example: I'm curious to know how the company supports its employees' work-life balance.
phrases.plain: I'd like to know how the company supports its employees' work-life balance.
phrases.note: Shows genuine interest and engagement. Makes your questions sound more natural.

phrases.meaning: Expresses formal or sincere happiness about information received.
phrases.example: I'm delighted to hear that your recovery is going so well after the surgery.
phrases.plain: I'm very happy to hear that your recovery is going so well after the surgery.
phrases.note: A slightly more formal or considered way to express happiness than "That's wonderful news."

phrases.meaning: A direct statement indicating that you have finished your contribution and others can speak.
phrases.example: That's all from me; I'm done speaking on this topic for now.
phrases.plain: That's all from me; I have finished my contribution on this topic for now.
phrases.note: Clear and direct way to signal the end of your turn, less common than "that's all."

phrases.meaning: To indicate that one has no strong preference and is happy with any choice.
phrases.example: Pizza or pasta? I'm easy, whatever you prefer.
phrases.plain: Pizza or pasta? I have no strong preference, whatever you prefer.
phrases.note: Informal. Means 'I don't mind' or 'I'm flexible'.

phrases.text: I'm feeling a bit under the weather
phrases.form: I'm feeling a bit under the weather
phrases.meaning: A polite way to say one is feeling slightly unwell or sick.
phrases.example: I'm feeling a bit under the weather, so I might skip the party tonight.
phrases.plain: I am feeling slightly unwell, so I might skip the party tonight.
phrases.note: Common and polite way to explain mild illness without going into detail.

phrases.meaning: Hearing your own voice or other sounds repeated back during the call.
phrases.example: I'm getting an echo on my end; could you check your microphone?
phrases.plain: I hear a repeated sound on my end; could you check your microphone?
phrases.note: Common problem on calls, often caused by an open microphone or speaker.

phrases.meaning: Expresses satisfaction that a situation or plan had a successful outcome.
phrases.example: Despite the initial challenges, I'm glad it worked out in the end.
phrases.plain: Despite the initial challenges, I'm happy it was successful in the end.
phrases.note: A common expression of relief and satisfaction after a successful resolution.

phrases.meaning: Expresses relief that a difficult or unpleasant situation has ended.
phrases.example: After weeks of intense negotiations, I'm glad that's over and we can move forward.
phrases.plain: After weeks of intense negotiations, I'm happy it's finished and we can move forward.
phrases.note: A common, informal expression of relief after a challenging period.

phrases.text: I'm glad to be of assistance
phrases.form: I'm glad to be of assistance
phrases.meaning: Expresses satisfaction and willingness to help after providing aid.
phrases.example: If you need anything else, just ask. I'm glad to be of assistance.
phrases.plain: If you need anything else, just ask. I'm happy to help.
phrases.note: A polite and slightly formal phrase used by someone who has provided help.

phrases.meaning: Expresses satisfaction and willingness to assist after providing aid.
phrases.example: I'm glad to have helped you with your presentation; it looks great now.
phrases.plain: I'm happy that I was able to assist you with your presentation; it looks great now.
phrases.note: A polite and common phrase used by someone who has provided assistance.

phrases.meaning: Expresses happiness or relief about receiving specific information.
phrases.example: I'm glad to know that the new security measures are already in place.
phrases.plain: I'm happy to know that the new security measures are already in place.
phrases.note: A common and polite way to acknowledge useful or reassuring information.

phrases.meaning: Expresses satisfaction and willingness to assist after providing aid.
phrases.example: I'm glad we could help you sort out the technical issues with your presentation.
phrases.plain: I'm happy that we were able to assist you with the technical issues with your presentation.
phrases.note: A polite and common phrase used by someone who has provided assistance.

phrases.meaning: Expresses satisfaction that a conversation took place, often resolving an issue.
phrases.example: I'm glad we talked about the project concerns; I feel much clearer now.
phrases.plain: I'm happy we discussed the project concerns; I feel much clearer now.
phrases.note: A common phrase used to conclude a conversation, especially one that was important or difficult.

phrases.text: I'm glad you brought that up
phrases.form: I'm glad you brought that up
phrases.meaning: Express appreciation that someone raised a particular topic or issue.
phrases.example: I'm glad you brought that up; it's an important point we need to discuss as a team.
phrases.plain: I'm happy you mentioned that; it's an important point we need to discuss as a team.
phrases.note: A positive way to acknowledge someone for raising a relevant issue.

phrases.text: I'm glad you could make it
phrases.form: I'm glad you could make it
phrases.meaning: A polite expression of pleasure that someone was able to attend.
phrases.example: Oh, you're here! I'm glad you could make it to the gathering.
phrases.plain: Oh, you're here! I am pleased you were able to attend the gathering.
phrases.note: Common and welcoming phrase from a host to a guest.

phrases.meaning: Express deep appreciation or thankfulness for something.
phrases.example: I'm grateful for your honest feedback; it helps me grow professionally.
phrases.plain: I appreciate your honest feedback; it helps me grow professionally.
phrases.note: A sincere way to express thanks, especially for valuable input.

phrases.meaning: To offer to provide a clearer explanation of something.
phrases.example: If anything was unclear, I'm happy to clarify any points.
phrases.plain: If anything was unclear, I'm willing to explain any points.
phrases.note: Shows willingness to ensure understanding. Collaborative and helpful.

phrases.meaning: To offer to organize or manage a task or activity.
phrases.example: If we need someone to manage the next steps, I'm happy to coordinate that.
phrases.plain: If we need someone to manage the next steps, I'm willing to organize that.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to take on a leadership or organizational role.

phrases.meaning: Offer to talk further about a topic or issue.
phrases.example: If you have more questions about the new policy, I'm happy to discuss them.
phrases.plain: If you have more questions about the new policy, I will gladly discuss them.
phrases.note: A polite and open offer to continue a conversation or provide more information.

phrases.meaning: To offer to take further action or investigate something after the meeting.
phrases.example: I'm happy to follow up with the client regarding their feedback.
phrases.plain: I'm willing to take further action with the client regarding their feedback.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to take responsibility for next steps. Collaborative.

phrases.meaning: Offer assistance or support willingly.
phrases.example: If you need any guidance on the new project, I'm happy to help.
phrases.plain: If you need any guidance on the new project, I will gladly assist you.
phrases.note: A common and polite way to offer support.

phrases.text: I'm happy to help with that
phrases.form: I'm happy to help with that
phrases.meaning: To offer assistance with a task or problem.
phrases.example: If you need someone to draft the report, I'm happy to help with that.
phrases.plain: If you need someone to draft the report, I'm willing to help.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to contribute. Collaborative and supportive.

phrases.meaning: To offer to give a presentation or share information.
phrases.example: If you'd like, I'm happy to present the latest sales figures.
phrases.plain: If you'd like, I'm willing to present the latest sales figures.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to take on a presentation role. Collaborative.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce positive news or a successful outcome.
phrases.example: I'm happy to report that the fundraising event exceeded all our expectations.
phrases.plain: I'm pleased to announce that the fundraising event exceeded all our expectations.
phrases.note: A formal or semi-formal way to deliver good news, often in a professional context.

phrases.meaning: Express pleasure or satisfaction about an observation or development.
phrases.example: I'm happy to see your proactive approach to problem-solving on this project.
phrases.plain: I'm pleased by your proactive approach to problem-solving on this project.
phrases.note: A positive and encouraging way to give feedback, often from a manager.

phrases.text: I'm happy to share my screen
phrases.form: I'm happy to share my screen
phrases.meaning: To offer to display your computer screen to others in a virtual meeting.
phrases.example: If it helps, I'm happy to share my screen to show the data.
phrases.plain: If it helps, I'm willing to show my screen to display the data.
phrases.note: Common phrase in online meetings. Collaborative and practical.

phrases.meaning: To volunteer to record the key points and decisions of the meeting.
phrases.example: If no one else is available, I'm happy to take notes for this session.
phrases.plain: If no one else is available, I'm willing to write down the meeting notes.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to contribute administratively. Collaborative.

phrases.meaning: To invite participants to ask questions after a presentation or explanation.
phrases.example: That concludes my presentation; I'm happy to take questions now.
phrases.plain: That concludes my presentation; I'm willing to answer questions now.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for inviting Q&A. Professional and open.

phrases.text: I'm happy to take that on
phrases.form: I'm happy to take that on
phrases.meaning: To volunteer to be responsible for a task or action.
phrases.example: That sounds like a good idea; I'm happy to take that on as an action point.
phrases.plain: That sounds like a good idea; I'm happy to be responsible for that task.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to accept responsibility. Collaborative tone.

phrases.text: I'm happy to take the lead
phrases.form: I'm happy to take the lead
phrases.meaning: To offer to be the main person responsible for a task or project.
phrases.example: If no one else is available, I'm happy to take the lead on this initiative.
phrases.plain: If no one else is available, I'm willing to be in charge of this initiative.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to assume leadership. Proactive and responsible.

phrases.meaning: To offer to do a task or take on a responsibility without being asked.
phrases.example: If you need someone to research this, I'm happy to volunteer.
phrases.plain: If you need someone to research this, I'm willing to offer my help.
phrases.note: Expresses willingness to contribute. Proactive and helpful.

phrases.meaning: Experiencing problems with the internet or phone signal that affect call quality.
phrases.example: I'm having connection issues, so my video might be a bit unstable today.
phrases.plain: My internet is unstable, so my video might be a bit unstable today.
phrases.note: A common and direct way to explain technical difficulties during a call.

phrases.meaning: Experiencing general problems with equipment or software during the call.
phrases.example: Please bear with me, I'm having technical difficulties with my camera.
phrases.plain: Please bear with me, my camera is not working correctly.
phrases.note: A general and polite way to explain any technical problem.

phrases.meaning: Used to state the purpose of your presence as presenting a strong case.
phrases.example: I'm here to argue that our current budget allocation is no longer effective.
phrases.plain: My purpose here is to show that our current budget allocation is no longer effective.
phrases.note: Direct and assertive, setting the stage for a persuasive presentation.

phrases.meaning: Offer help and encouragement to someone.
phrases.example: As you implement these changes, remember I'm here to support you every step of the way.
phrases.plain: As you implement these changes, remember I will help you every step of the way.
phrases.note: A common, reassuring phrase from a manager or mentor offering assistance.

phrases.meaning: Express admiration for someone's skill, effort, or achievement.
phrases.example: I'm impressed by how quickly you adapted to the new software, despite the steep learning curve.
phrases.plain: I admire how quickly you adapted to the new software, despite it being difficult to learn.
phrases.note: A direct and sincere way to give praise.

phrases.meaning: Express admiration for someone's qualities or achievements.
phrases.example: I'm impressed with your ability to manage multiple tasks effectively.
phrases.plain: I admire your ability to manage multiple tasks effectively.
phrases.note: A sincere way to give praise, focusing on a skill or quality.

phrases.meaning: A very informal and quick way to accept an invitation or agree to participate.
phrases.example: A spontaneous road trip this weekend? I'm in!
phrases.plain: A spontaneous road trip this weekend? I'll participate!
phrases.note: Highly informal and enthusiastic. Used among close friends.

phrases.meaning: Used to express a tendency to concur with an idea or statement.
phrases.example: I'm inclined to agree that a more collaborative approach is needed.
phrases.plain: I tend to agree that a more collaborative approach is needed.
phrases.note: A polite way to express agreement, often with a slight reservation.

phrases.meaning: Expressing a tendency towards a particular opinion or belief.
phrases.example: I'm inclined to think that a different strategy might yield better results.
phrases.plain: I tend to think that a different strategy might yield better results.
phrases.note: A polite and slightly tentative way to offer an alternative perspective.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are very close to finishing a task.
phrases.example: I'm just about done with this report, then I can join you.
phrases.plain: I'm almost finished with this report, then I can join you.
phrases.note: Useful for coordinating activities or managing expectations about your availability.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are very close to completing a specific task.
phrases.example: I'm just about done with this email, then I'm free.
phrases.plain: I'm almost finished with this email, then I'm free.
phrases.note: Specific version of 'I'm just about done'. Useful for managing expectations.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are almost prepared for something.
phrases.example: Give me five minutes, I'm just about ready to go.
phrases.plain: Give me five minutes, I'm almost prepared to go.
phrases.note: Common for coordinating departures or starting activities.

phrases.text: I'm just about to call it a day
phrases.form: I'm just about to call it a day
phrases.meaning: An informal way to say you are about to stop working for the day.
phrases.example: I'm just about to call it a day, I'm exhausted.
phrases.plain: I'm going to stop working for the day very soon, I'm exhausted.
phrases.note: Very common and casual. Signals the end of the workday.

phrases.text: I'm just about to call it a night
phrases.form: I'm just about to call it a night
phrases.meaning: An informal way to say you are about to stop an activity or go to bed for the evening.
phrases.example: It's getting late, I'm just about to call it a night.
phrases.plain: It's getting late, I'm going to stop my activities for the evening.
phrases.note: Very common and casual. Signals the end of the evening's activities.

phrases.text: I'm just about to get started on
phrases.form: I'm just about to get started on
phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of beginning a specific task or project.
phrases.example: I'm just about to get started on the quarterly report.
phrases.plain: I'm going to begin the quarterly report very soon.
phrases.note: Emphasizes the initiation of a particular task. Very common.

phrases.text: I'm just about to grab some lunch
phrases.form: I'm just about to grab some lunch
phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are about to go and eat lunch.
phrases.example: I'm just about to grab some lunch, want to join me?
phrases.plain: I'm going to get some lunch very soon, want to join me?
phrases.note: Common and casual. Can be an invitation or an explanation for leaving.

phrases.text: I'm just about to head home
phrases.form: I'm just about to head home
phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of leaving to go home.
phrases.example: It's late, I'm just about to head home.
phrases.plain: It's late, I'm going to leave for home very soon.
phrases.note: A clear signal that you are departing for the day. Very common.

phrases.text: I'm just about to head out
phrases.form: I'm just about to head out
