phrases.note: Similar to "I'm a bit concerned," but focuses on the situation itself rather than personal feeling.

phrases.meaning: Used to state that something happens frequently or is not unusual.
phrases.example: Losing your luggage on a long trip, unfortunately, it's a common occurrence.
phrases.plain: Losing your luggage on a long trip, unfortunately, happens frequently.
phrases.note: Describes something as a regular or expected event, often with a neutral tone.

phrases.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a reasonable and justifiable observation.
phrases.example: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's a fair point about the timeline.
phrases.plain: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's a reasonable observation about the timeline.
phrases.note: Similar to 'good point,' but often implies a concession or understanding.

phrases.meaning: Used to state that something is an accepted fact or a fundamental assumption.
phrases.example: It's a given that we'll need to work extra hours to meet the deadline.
phrases.plain: It's an accepted fact that we'll need to work extra hours to meet the deadline.
phrases.note: Implies that a point is so obvious or fundamental it doesn't need discussion.

phrases.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a valid and relevant observation.
phrases.example: You're right, we haven't considered the budget. That's a good point.
phrases.plain: You're right, we haven't considered the budget. That's a valid observation.
phrases.note: A common way to agree with or acknowledge the value of someone's contribution.

phrases.meaning: Used to state that something is objectively true and not open to debate.
phrases.example: The earth is round; it's a matter of fact, not a belief.
phrases.plain: The earth is round; it's objectively true, not a belief.
phrases.note: Contrasts with 'matter of opinion,' asserting objective truth.

phrases.meaning: Used to state that something is subjective and open to different viewpoints.
phrases.example: Whether that design is good or bad, it's a matter of opinion, really.
phrases.plain: Whether that design is good or bad, it's subjective, really.
phrases.note: Emphasizes that there is no single correct answer or universal agreement.

phrases.meaning: Used to express that something is inevitable and will happen eventually.
phrases.example: With all the changes, it's a matter of time before the company restructures.
phrases.plain: With all the changes, it's inevitable that the company will restructure eventually.
phrases.note: Suggests certainty about a future event, often with a sense of anticipation.

phrases.meaning: Expresses regret or sadness about a missed opportunity or an unfortunate situation.
phrases.example: It's a pity we didn't get to see the exhibition before it closed last week.
phrases.plain: It's regrettable we didn't get to see the exhibition before it closed last week.
phrases.note: A common way to express mild regret or sadness. Similar to "It's a shame."

phrases.meaning: Used to express regret or sadness about a situation.
phrases.example: It's a pity that we couldn't spend more time together on your visit.
phrases.plain: It's regrettable that we couldn't spend more time together on your visit.
phrases.note: Similar to 'it's a shame that,' expressing mild regret or sorrow.

phrases.meaning: Used to state that something happens infrequently or is unusual.
phrases.example: Getting everyone together for dinner these days, it's a rare occasion.
phrases.plain: Getting everyone together for dinner these days, it happens infrequently.
phrases.note: Highlights the infrequency or special nature of an event.

phrases.meaning: Expresses regret or mild disappointment about a situation.
phrases.example: It's a shame we couldn't get tickets for the concert, it sold out so fast.
phrases.plain: It's disappointing we couldn't get tickets for the concert, it sold out so fast.
phrases.note: Very similar to "That's a shame," used interchangeably.

phrases.meaning: Used to express regret or disappointment about a situation.
phrases.example: It's a shame that the event was cancelled due to bad weather.
phrases.plain: It's disappointing that the event was cancelled due to bad weather.
phrases.note: Conveys a sense of regret for an unfortunate or missed opportunity.

phrases.meaning: An expression used when you discover an unexpected connection with someone.
phrases.example: You know my cousin? Wow, it's a small world!
phrases.plain: You know my cousin? Wow, what an unexpected connection!
phrases.note: Common and friendly. Expresses surprise at coincidences.

phrases.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a logically sound and well-reasoned observation.
phrases.example: You're right, the data does support that conclusion. That's a valid point.
phrases.plain: You're right, the data does support that conclusion. That's a logically sound observation.
phrases.note: Emphasizes the logical strength and correctness of an argument.

phrases.meaning: A common phrase to explain why you might be tired or haven't done much else.
phrases.example: I haven't had time for hobbies, it's been a busy week at work.
phrases.plain: I haven't had time for hobbies, my work week was very active.
phrases.note: Relatable and often used as a mild excuse or explanation for lack of free time.

phrases.meaning: A polite way to say goodbye, indicating you enjoyed the interaction.
phrases.example: Well, I must be going. It's been a pleasure chatting with you.
phrases.plain: Well, I must be going. I enjoyed chatting with you.
phrases.note: A polite and slightly formal way to end a conversation, especially with new acquaintances.

phrases.text: It's been a pleasure chatting with you
phrases.form: It's been a pleasure chatting with you
phrases.meaning: A polite closing remark when ending a casual conversation.
phrases.example: Well, I should go. It's been a pleasure chatting with you.
phrases.plain: Well, I should go. I enjoyed our casual conversation.
phrases.note: Friendly and polite. Suitable for informal interactions with acquaintances.

phrases.text: It's been a pleasure having you
phrases.form: It's been a pleasure having you
phrases.meaning: A polite closing remark from a host to a guest, indicating enjoyment of their visit.
phrases.example: Thanks for coming, it's been a pleasure having you over.
phrases.plain: Thanks for coming, I enjoyed your visit.
phrases.note: Used by a host. Polite and warm. Suitable for social gatherings.

phrases.text: It's been a pleasure meeting you
phrases.form: It's been a pleasure meeting you
phrases.meaning: A polite closing remark when ending a conversation with someone you met for the first time.
phrases.example: Well, I must go. It's been a pleasure meeting you, Sarah.
phrases.plain: Well, I must go. I enjoyed meeting you, Sarah.
phrases.note: Standard polite farewell for new acquaintances. Slightly more formal than 'talking to you'.

phrases.text: It's been a pleasure working alongside you
phrases.form: It's been a pleasure working alongside you
phrases.meaning: A polite closing remark, especially when a collaborative project ends.
phrases.example: As the project concludes, it's been a pleasure working alongside you.
phrases.plain: As the project concludes, I enjoyed collaborating with you.
phrases.note: Professional and polite. Emphasizes collaboration. Slightly more formal.

phrases.text: It's been a pleasure working with you
phrases.form: It's been a pleasure working with you
phrases.meaning: A polite closing remark, especially when a project or collaboration ends.
phrases.example: As this project wraps up, it's been a pleasure working with you all.
phrases.plain: As this project wraps up, I enjoyed working with you all.
phrases.note: Professional and polite. Good for ending a work-related interaction.

phrases.meaning: A common phrase to express satisfaction with what you've accomplished.
phrases.example: I managed to finish three reports, it's been a productive day.
phrases.plain: I managed to finish three reports, this day was very fruitful.
phrases.note: Positive and professional. Good for light conversation about work.

phrases.meaning: Used to acknowledge that a significant amount of time has passed since last meeting.
phrases.example: Wow, it's been a while since we last saw each other!
phrases.plain: Wow, a long time has passed since we last saw each other!
phrases.note: A friendly way to start a conversation with someone you haven't seen in ages.

phrases.meaning: Used to acknowledge that a long time has passed since a particular event.
phrases.example: It's been a while since I last visited my hometown.
phrases.plain: A long time has passed since I last visited my hometown.
phrases.note: Common for reminiscing or explaining a gap in activity.

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say a very long time has passed since the last meeting.
phrases.example: Wow, it's been ages since we last had coffee together.
phrases.plain: Wow, a very long time has passed since we last had coffee together.
phrases.note: Common and informal, expressing surprise or emphasis on the time passed.

phrases.meaning: Used to state something that is obvious or easily understood.
phrases.example: It's clear that we need to improve our online presence to attract new customers.
phrases.plain: We obviously need to improve our online presence to attract new customers.
phrases.note: Presents a conclusion as undeniable, aiming for agreement.

phrases.meaning: Used to emphasize the extreme importance or necessity of something.
phrases.example: It's crucial that we secure this funding to keep the project on track.
phrases.plain: We absolutely must secure this funding to keep the project on track.
phrases.note: Strong and direct, used when the outcome depends heavily on the action.

phrases.meaning: Emphasizing the extreme importance of a particular action.
phrases.example: It's crucial that we learn from our mistakes and improve our processes.
phrases.plain: We must learn from our mistakes and improve our processes.
phrases.note: Used to stress the vital importance of an action.

phrases.meaning: Used to emphasize the absolute necessity of an action or condition.
phrases.example: It's essential to maintain open communication channels during the merger.
phrases.plain: It is absolutely necessary to maintain open communication channels during the merger.
phrases.note: Stronger than 'important', indicating a critical requirement.

phrases.meaning: to describe the fundamental nature of something in a simplified way.
phrases.example: It's essentially a new way of managing our customer relationships more efficiently.
phrases.plain: It's a new way of managing our customer relationships more efficiently.
phrases.note: Used to provide a basic, core description.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is generally accepted as true or reasonable.
phrases.example: It's fair to say that the project faced unexpected challenges.
phrases.plain: It is reasonable to say that the project faced unexpected challenges.
phrases.note: Suggests a balanced and objective assessment.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that you believe is reasonable and generally accepted.
phrases.example: It's fair to say that the project exceeded expectations despite initial challenges.
phrases.plain: The project exceeded expectations despite initial challenges.
phrases.note: A common way to express a reasonable conclusion or observation.

phrases.meaning: A friendly expression used when you've had a chance to talk and share news.
phrases.example: Well, it's good to catch up, let's do it again soon.
phrases.plain: Well, it's good to talk and share news, let's do it again soon.
phrases.note: Common closing remark after a conversation with someone you haven't seen in a while.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that a visual, sensory, or abstract experience is difficult to put into words.
phrases.example: The view from the mountain was incredible; it's hard to describe how beautiful it was.
phrases.plain: The view from the mountain was incredible; it's difficult to put into words how beautiful it was.
phrases.note: Commonly used for subjective experiences like beauty, taste, or feelings.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that a concept or situation is difficult to articulate clearly.
phrases.example: It's hard to explain, but I just had a bad feeling about the whole thing.
phrases.plain: It's difficult to articulate, but I just had a bad feeling about the whole thing.
phrases.note: Often used when describing an intuition or a complex emotional state.

phrases.meaning: Emphasizing the absolute necessity and urgency of an action.
phrases.example: It's imperative that we meet the deadline for this critical project.
phrases.plain: We absolutely must meet the deadline for this critical project.
phrases.note: Strongest emphasis on necessity and urgency.

phrases.meaning: Emphasize the significance or necessity of a particular action or consideration.
phrases.example: It's important to acknowledge the hard work everyone put into this successful launch.
phrases.plain: We must acknowledge the hard work everyone put into this successful launch.
phrases.note: Used to highlight the significance of something, often when giving praise or advice.

phrases.meaning: Used to recognize and accept a fact or truth, often a limitation or counter-argument.
phrases.example: It's important to acknowledge that there are limitations to this methodology.
phrases.plain: We must acknowledge that there are limitations to this methodology.
phrases.note: Shows intellectual honesty and strengthens an argument by addressing weaknesses.

phrases.meaning: Used to highlight a crucial factor or aspect that needs attention.
phrases.example: It's important to consider the ethical implications of using AI in this context.
phrases.plain: We must consider the ethical implications of using AI in this context.
phrases.note: A strong way to introduce a significant point for discussion or analysis.

phrases.meaning: Used to emphasize the need to differentiate two concepts or ideas.
phrases.example: It's important to distinguish between correlation and causation in this context.
phrases.plain: We must differentiate between correlation and causation in this context.
phrases.note: Crucial for clarity and precision in academic arguments.

phrases.meaning: Used to draw attention to a significant piece of information.
phrases.example: It's important to note that this decision will affect all departments equally.
phrases.plain: We should pay attention to the fact that this decision will affect all departments equally.
phrases.note: Highlights a crucial detail that might otherwise be overlooked.

phrases.meaning: Used to highlight a significant piece of information or a detail that should be remembered.
phrases.example: It's important to note that these findings are specific to this demographic.
phrases.plain: These findings are specific to this demographic.
phrases.note: A common way to draw attention to a crucial detail or limitation.

phrases.meaning: Used to stress the significance of a particular fact or detail.
phrases.example: It's important to remember that our clients value reliability above all else.
phrases.plain: We must remember that our clients value reliability above all else.
phrases.note: Emphasizes a key point that should not be forgotten.

phrases.meaning: Emphasizing a crucial piece of information or a key consideration.
phrases.example: It's important to remember that our clients rely on our timely delivery.
phrases.plain: We must remember that our clients rely on our timely delivery.
phrases.note: Used to highlight a significant point.

phrases.meaning: to emphasize the significance of a particular piece of information.
phrases.example: It's important to understand that market conditions can change rapidly.
phrases.plain: Market conditions can change rapidly.
phrases.note: Used to stress a crucial point for comprehension.

phrases.meaning: A more informal way to introduce a comparison or analogy to help explain something.
phrases.example: This new software, it's kind of like a simplified version of the old one.
phrases.plain: This new software is similar to a simplified version of the old one.
phrases.note: Very common in casual conversation to offer a quick, informal comparison.

phrases.meaning: Used to express that something is not surprising, given the circumstances.
phrases.example: He worked 70 hours a week; it's no wonder he's feeling burnt out.
phrases.plain: He worked 70 hours a week; it's not surprising he's feeling burnt out.
phrases.note: Connects a cause to an expected effect, often with a sense of inevitability.

phrases.meaning: Expresses that a situation is less than perfect or has drawbacks, often politely.
phrases.example: Having to reschedule the meeting at such short notice, it's not ideal for everyone's calendars.
phrases.plain: Having to reschedule the meeting at such short notice, it's inconvenient for everyone's calendars.
phrases.note: A polite and understated way to express dissatisfaction or acknowledge a less-than-perfect situation.

phrases.meaning: Used to clarify a point by stating what is not the main reason or issue.
phrases.example: It's not so much that the theory is wrong, but rather that it's incomplete.
phrases.plain: The theory isn't wrong, but it's incomplete.
phrases.note: Useful for nuanced explanations, distinguishing between primary and secondary issues.

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say that one will pay for something.
phrases.example: Don't worry about the bill, it's on me tonight.
phrases.plain: Don't worry about the bill, I will pay for it tonight.
phrases.note: Informal and friendly way to offer to pay, often for a round of drinks or a meal.

phrases.meaning: Used to describe a situation that is unavoidable, inexplicable, or simply part of life.
phrases.example: The flight was delayed again. Oh well, it's one of those things, I guess.
phrases.plain: The flight was delayed again. Oh well, it's an unavoidable part of life, I guess.
phrases.note: A resigned way to accept a common or frustrating situation.

phrases.meaning: Used to emphasize that something is absolutely necessary for success or survival.
phrases.example: It's vital that we secure additional funding for the next phase.
phrases.plain: It is absolutely necessary that we secure additional funding for the next phase.
phrases.note: A very strong way to express necessity. More emphatic than 'important'.

phrases.meaning: Emphasizing the extreme importance and necessity of an action.
phrases.example: It's vital that we learn from this experience and adapt quickly.
phrases.plain: We must learn from this experience and adapt quickly.
phrases.note: Stronger than 'essential', stresses absolute necessity.

phrases.meaning: Used to suggest that an idea or option should be given serious thought.
phrases.example: It's worth considering a flexible work schedule to improve staff morale.
phrases.plain: We should think seriously about a flexible work schedule to improve staff morale.
phrases.note: A gentle way to introduce a suggestion without being too forceful.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a point that deserves thought or attention.
phrases.example: It's worth considering that these results might not be generalizable to other populations.
phrases.plain: We should consider that these results might not be generalizable to other populations.
phrases.note: A polite way to suggest an important factor for evaluation.

phrases.text: It's worth considering the fact that
phrases.form: It's worth considering the fact that
phrases.meaning: Used to introduce an important piece of information that should be taken into account.
phrases.example: It's worth considering the fact that the sample size was relatively small.
phrases.plain: We should consider that the sample size was relatively small.
phrases.note: A slightly more formal version of 'It's worth considering that'.

phrases.meaning: to highlight an important piece of information that should be remembered.
phrases.example: It's worth noting that the initial budget estimates were quite conservative.
phrases.plain: The initial budget estimates were quite conservative.
phrases.note: Draws attention to a significant detail.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce an important piece of information or a detail that should be remembered.
phrases.example: It's worth noting that these findings are preliminary and require further validation.
phrases.plain: These findings are preliminary and require further validation.
phrases.note: A common way to highlight a significant point in a discussion or presentation.

phrases.text: It's worth noting the difference between
phrases.form: It's worth noting the difference between
phrases.meaning: Used to highlight the distinction between two things.
phrases.example: It's worth noting the difference between theoretical and practical applications.
phrases.plain: We should note the difference between theoretical and practical applications.
phrases.note: A polite way to draw attention to a crucial distinction.

phrases.meaning: Used to draw attention to a specific detail or fact that is important.
phrases.example: It's worth pointing out that these results are preliminary and not yet peer-reviewed.
phrases.plain: These results are preliminary and not yet peer-reviewed.
phrases.note: A common way to highlight a crucial piece of information or a caveat.

phrases.meaning: Used to suggest that a specific piece of information is valuable to keep in mind.
phrases.example: It's worth remembering that market conditions can change rapidly.
phrases.plain: Remember that market conditions can change rapidly.
phrases.note: A gentle but firm way to highlight an important consideration. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to remind someone of an important fact or detail.
phrases.example: It's worth remembering that correlation does not imply causation.
phrases.plain: Remember that correlation does not imply causation.
phrases.note: A polite way to bring an important point back into focus.

phrases.meaning: extreme tiredness and other physical effects felt after a long flight across time zones.
phrases.example: I'm still suffering from jet lag after my flight from Australia.
phrases.plain: I'm still suffering from tiredness after my long flight across time zones.
phrases.note: Common after long-haul flights.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a brief, concise comment or piece of information.
phrases.example: Just a quick point on the budget: we need to factor in shipping costs.
phrases.plain: I have a brief comment on the budget: we need to factor in shipping costs.
phrases.note: Informal and common way to add a short, relevant piece of information.

phrases.meaning: Used to present an idea or suggestion in a casual, non-committal way.
phrases.example: We could offer a discount for early registration, just a thought.
phrases.plain: We could offer a discount for early registration; it's an idea.
phrases.note: Informal, used to float an idea without strong commitment.

phrases.meaning: a very short distance away.
phrases.example: Don't worry, the train station is just around the corner from here.
phrases.plain: Don't worry, the train station is very close to here.
phrases.note: Informal way to indicate proximity.

phrases.meaning: Used to describe an event that happened at the exact moment another action was taking place.
phrases.example: Just as I was falling asleep, I heard a loud noise outside.
phrases.plain: At the exact moment I was falling asleep, I heard a loud noise outside.
phrases.note: Connects two simultaneous events, often one interrupting the other.

phrases.meaning: Used to ensure understanding or to clarify a point, often before giving feedback.
phrases.example: Just to be clear, I think the content is strong, but the formatting needs some adjustments.
phrases.plain: I want to make sure you understand: the content is strong, but the formatting needs adjustments.
phrases.note: Used to preface a clarification or to ensure no misunderstanding.

phrases.meaning: Used to ask for or provide a clearer explanation of something.
phrases.example: Just to clarify, are we talking about the first or second quarter results?
phrases.plain: To make it clear, are we talking about the first or second quarter results?
phrases.note: Common phrase for seeking or offering precision. Neutral and professional.

phrases.meaning: To monitor or watch something carefully.
phrases.example: I'll keep an eye on the budget to ensure we don't overspend.
phrases.plain: I'll monitor the budget to ensure we don't overspend.
phrases.note: A common, informal way to say you will monitor something.

phrases.meaning: To monitor a general situation or overall progress.
phrases.example: I'll keep an eye on things while you're away next week.
phrases.plain: I'll monitor the situation while you're away next week.
phrases.note: A general way to say you will supervise or monitor.

phrases.meaning: To watch carefully for something or someone.
phrases.example: Please keep an eye out for any potential issues during the testing phase.
phrases.plain: Please watch carefully for any potential issues during the testing phase.
phrases.note: Used for vigilance or anticipation of problems.

phrases.meaning: To be willing to consider new ideas or opinions without prejudice.
phrases.example: Let's keep an open mind when evaluating the unconventional proposals.
phrases.plain: Let's be willing to consider new ideas when evaluating the unconventional proposals.
phrases.note: Encourages receptiveness to different perspectives.

phrases.meaning: Used to remind someone of an important fact or consideration.
phrases.example: Keep in mind that our competitors are also developing similar products.
phrases.plain: Remember that our competitors are also developing similar products.
phrases.note: A gentle reminder, often used to add context to an argument.

phrases.meaning: To maintain communication with someone, usually informally.
phrases.example: It was great seeing you, let's promise to keep in touch more often.
phrases.plain: It was great seeing you, let's promise to communicate more often.
phrases.note: Common farewell, encouraging continued communication.

phrases.meaning: To keep someone informed about developments or progress.
phrases.example: Please keep me in the loop regarding any changes to the project schedule.
phrases.plain: Please keep me informed about any changes to the project schedule.
phrases.note: A common, informal request to stay updated.

phrases.meaning: To keep someone informed about developments or progress.
phrases.example: Please keep me posted on the progress of the negotiations.
phrases.plain: Please keep me informed about the progress of the negotiations.
phrases.note: A common, informal request to stay updated.

phrases.meaning: To ensure that progress continues without unnecessary delays.
phrases.example: We need to make quick decisions to keep things moving forward.
phrases.plain: We need to make quick decisions to ensure progress continues.
phrases.note: Used to emphasize maintaining momentum.

phrases.meaning: To ensure that operations continue without problems or interruptions.
phrases.example: We need to implement new protocols to keep things running smoothly.
phrases.plain: We need to implement new protocols to ensure operations continue without problems.
phrases.note: Used for maintaining efficient and problem-free operations.

phrases.meaning: To monitor or follow the progress or whereabouts of something.
phrases.example: It's important to keep track of our expenses to avoid overspending.
phrases.plain: It's important to monitor our expenses to avoid overspending.
phrases.note: Used for ongoing monitoring of data or progress.

phrases.meaning: Encourage someone to continue performing at their current high standard.
phrases.example: Your analysis was excellent this quarter, so keep up the good work.
phrases.plain: Your analysis was excellent this quarter; continue doing well.
phrases.note: A common, encouraging phrase, often used by managers.

phrases.meaning: The most important results or discoveries from research or analysis.
phrases.example: Let's now discuss the key findings of our recent customer survey.
phrases.plain: Let's now discuss the most important results of our recent customer survey.
phrases.note: Standard academic and business terminology. Professional and clear.

phrases.meaning: States an intention to review and adjust audio or video configurations.
phrases.example: I can't hear you, let me check my settings quickly.
phrases.plain: I can't hear you, I will quickly review my settings.
phrases.note: Common response when troubleshooting personal audio/video issues.

phrases.meaning: to offer to make an explanation clearer.
phrases.example: Some people seemed confused, so let me clarify the new expense reporting procedure.
phrases.plain: Some people seemed confused, so I will make the new expense reporting procedure clearer.
phrases.note: Polite way to offer further explanation.

phrases.meaning: Used to explain something more clearly or correct a potential misunderstanding.
phrases.example: I think there's a misunderstanding, so let me clarify that point for everyone.
phrases.plain: I think there's a misunderstanding, so I will explain that point more clearly for everyone.
phrases.note: Useful for ensuring accuracy and preventing confusion in discussions.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate that you are about to fix an error in your previous statement.
phrases.example: Actually, let me correct myself; the figures are from last quarter, not this one.
phrases.plain: Actually, the figures are from last quarter, not this one.
phrases.note: A direct and clear way to acknowledge and fix an error. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to offer more details or a fuller explanation of a previous point.
phrases.example: Let me elaborate on the reasons behind our decision to change suppliers.
phrases.plain: I will provide more details about why we decided to change suppliers.
phrases.note: Polite and professional way to expand on an idea. Often used in Q&A.

phrases.meaning: to offer to provide a detailed explanation.
phrases.example: I know it sounds complicated, but let me explain how the new system works.
phrases.plain: I know it sounds complicated, but I will explain how the new system works.
phrases.note: Direct and polite way to begin an explanation.

phrases.meaning: A request to be allowed to complete one's thought or argument without interruption.
phrases.example: Please, let me finish my point before you respond to my proposal.
phrases.plain: Please, allow me to complete my thought before you respond to my proposal.
phrases.note: Used when someone is being interrupted and wants to continue speaking. Can be firm.

phrases.meaning: A polite request to be allowed to complete your current thought or sentence.
phrases.example: If you don't mind, let me just finish this sentence, then I'll hear your thoughts.
phrases.plain: If you don't mind, allow me to complete this sentence, then I'll hear your thoughts.
phrases.note: Used when you are being interrupted and want to conclude your statement.

phrases.meaning: to invite the listener to ask questions or provide feedback.
phrases.example: I've covered the main points, but let me know if anything needs further clarification.
phrases.plain: I've covered the main points, but tell me if anything needs further clarification.
phrases.note: Polite and open invitation for questions.

phrases.meaning: Used to offer help or invite someone to inform you about something.
phrases.example: Let me know if you need any help with the presentation.
phrases.plain: Tell me if you need any help with the presentation.
phrases.note: A polite and helpful offer. Encourages communication.

phrases.text: let me put it this way
phrases.form: Let me put it this way
phrases.meaning: to introduce a different, often more direct or impactful, way of explaining something.
phrases.example: Let me put it this way: if we don't adapt, we risk becoming irrelevant in the market.
phrases.plain: If we don't adapt, we risk becoming irrelevant in the market.
phrases.note: Often used to deliver a more forceful or clear message.

phrases.text: Let me put that another way
phrases.form: Let me put that another way
phrases.meaning: Used to rephrase something you've said, often to make it clearer or more understandable.
phrases.example: That explanation was a bit convoluted; let me put that another way.
phrases.plain: That explanation was a bit convoluted; I will explain it differently.
phrases.note: Useful when you realize your initial explanation wasn't clear enough. Professional.

phrases.meaning: to say something again in a different way to make it clearer.
phrases.example: Let me rephrase that: the new policy applies to all employees, not just new hires.
phrases.plain: The new policy applies to all employees, not just new hires.
phrases.note: Used when you feel your initial explanation wasn't clear enough.

phrases.meaning: Expresses an intention to attempt to connect again, usually by phone.
phrases.example: The video isn't working, so let me try calling you on your mobile instead.
phrases.plain: The video isn't working, so I will call you on your mobile instead.
phrases.note: Used when switching communication methods due to technical problems.

phrases.meaning: to guide someone step-by-step through a process or explanation.
phrases.example: Let me walk you through the new onboarding process for remote employees.
phrases.plain: I will guide you through the new onboarding process for remote employees.
phrases.note: Used when explaining a procedure in detail.

phrases.meaning: Used to state something directly and unambiguously, often to avoid misunderstanding.
phrases.example: Let's be clear: our priority is long-term growth, not short-term profits.
phrases.plain: To be unambiguous: our priority is long-term growth, not short-term profits.
phrases.note: Direct and assertive, used to establish a definitive position.

phrases.meaning: Suggests ending the work or discussion for the current day.
phrases.example: We've made good progress, so let's call it a day and pick this up tomorrow.
phrases.plain: We've made good progress, so let's finish for today and continue this tomorrow.
phrases.note: Informal and common phrase to suggest ending work or a meeting.

phrases.meaning: Suggestion to meet and talk about recent events in each other's lives.
phrases.example: It's been too long, let's catch up properly over dinner soon.
phrases.plain: It's been too long, let's meet and talk about our lives over dinner soon.
phrases.note: Very common and friendly. Implies a desire for a longer, more personal conversation.

phrases.meaning: To return to a previous topic or issue later in the discussion.
phrases.example: That's an important point, but let's circle back to it after we discuss the budget.
phrases.plain: That's an important point, but let's return to it after we discuss the budget.
phrases.note: Common in business English for deferring a topic. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to invite others to think about a particular idea or option.
phrases.example: Let's consider the long-term implications of this decision before we proceed.
phrases.plain: We should think about the long-term implications of this decision before we proceed.
phrases.note: Collaborative and open, encourages group deliberation.

phrases.meaning: To investigate different possibilities or choices.
phrases.example: Before committing, let's explore options for reducing the overall project cost.
phrases.plain: Before committing, we should investigate different possibilities for reducing the overall project cost.
phrases.note: Encourages a thorough review of alternatives.

phrases.meaning: Suggest directing attention and effort towards a specific area or task.
phrases.example: For the next quarter, let's focus on improving our customer satisfaction scores.
phrases.plain: For the next quarter, we should concentrate on improving our customer satisfaction scores.
phrases.note: A common way to guide a team or individual towards a specific goal.

phrases.meaning: To suggest starting the main discussion immediately without delay.
phrases.example: We have a packed agenda, so let's get straight to it.
phrases.plain: We have a packed agenda, so let's start immediately.
phrases.note: Informal but common way to begin efficiently. Used by the chair.

phrases.meaning: To express a desire to complete a task or discussion efficiently.
phrases.example: We've discussed enough; let's get this done and move to implementation.
phrases.plain: We've discussed enough; let's complete this and move to implementation.
phrases.note: Motivating phrase, often used to encourage action. Informal but common.

phrases.meaning: Choosing a particular option or plan from several possibilities.
phrases.example: After reviewing everything, I think let's go with option B for now.
phrases.plain: After reviewing everything, I think we should choose option B for now.
phrases.note: A common, informal way to express a decision or preference.

phrases.meaning: To encourage all participants to share their views or input.
phrases.example: Before we decide, let's hear from everyone on this important matter.
phrases.plain: Before we decide, let's get everyone's opinion on this important matter.
phrases.note: Promotes inclusive discussion. Often used by the meeting leader.

phrases.meaning: To encourage participants to be receptive to new ideas or perspectives.
phrases.example: This is a new approach, so let's keep an open mind during the discussion.
phrases.plain: This is a new approach, so let's be receptive to new ideas during the discussion.
phrases.note: Promotes constructive and unbiased discussion. Collaborative.

phrases.meaning: To suggest that a discussion or presentation should be short and to the point.
phrases.example: We have a lot to cover, so let's keep it brief on each item.
phrases.plain: We have a lot to cover, so let's be concise on each item.
phrases.note: Used to manage time and focus. Can be said by the chair or a participant.

phrases.meaning: To suggest that contributions or discussions should be brief and to the point.
phrases.example: We have limited time, so let's keep it concise when sharing updates.
phrases.plain: We have limited time, so let's be brief when sharing updates.
phrases.note: Used to manage time and focus. Professional and efficient.

phrases.meaning: To encourage the discussion to progress and avoid getting stuck on one point.
phrases.example: We're short on time, so let's keep it moving to the next topic.
phrases.plain: We're short on time, so let's continue to the next topic.
phrases.note: Informal but common way to maintain pace. Used by the chair.

phrases.meaning: To encourage a constructive and optimistic tone in the discussion.
phrases.example: I know there are challenges, but let's keep it positive and focus on solutions.
phrases.plain: I know there are challenges, but let's stay optimistic and focus on solutions.
phrases.note: Used to manage the tone of the meeting. Encourages constructive dialogue.

phrases.meaning: To encourage continued progress and enthusiasm.
phrases.example: We've had a productive discussion, so let's keep the momentum going into next week.
phrases.plain: We've had a productive discussion, so let's continue this progress next week.
phrases.note: Motivating phrase. Used to maintain energy and productivity.

phrases.meaning: To remind participants to stay on topic and avoid digressions.
phrases.example: I appreciate the input, but let's keep this discussion focused on the budget.
phrases.plain: I appreciate the input, but let's keep this discussion only about the budget.
phrases.note: Used by the chair to maintain control and efficiency. Professional.

phrases.text: Let's look at it this way
phrases.form: Let's look at it this way
phrases.meaning: Used to introduce an alternative perspective or a re-framing of an issue.
phrases.example: Let's look at it this way: what's the worst-case scenario if we proceed?
phrases.plain: Consider it from this perspective: what's the worst-case scenario if we proceed?
phrases.note: Encourages a different viewpoint to aid understanding or persuasion.

phrases.meaning: A suggestion to arrange a specific time and activity to meet.
phrases.example: It's been too long, let's make a plan to get together next month.
phrases.plain: It's been too long, let's arrange a specific time to get together next month.
phrases.note: Friendly and proactive way to initiate concrete plans.

phrases.meaning: Suggest transitioning to the next topic or agenda item.
phrases.example: Now that we've discussed the budget, let's move on to the marketing strategy.
phrases.plain: Now that we've discussed the budget, let's proceed to the marketing strategy.
phrases.note: A common phrase for guiding a discussion or meeting.

phrases.meaning: To suggest discussing a specific topic outside of the current meeting.
phrases.example: That's a detailed issue, so let's move this offline to discuss further.
phrases.plain: That's a detailed issue, so let's discuss this outside of the meeting.
phrases.note: Common in business for managing time and relevance. Professional.

phrases.meaning: Used to remind people of an important fact or consideration.
phrases.example: Let's not forget the initial goals we set for this project when discussing changes.
phrases.plain: We should remember the initial goals we set for this project when discussing changes.
phrases.note: A gentle way to bring a forgotten but relevant point back into discussion.

phrases.text: Let's put a pin in that
phrases.form: Let's put a pin in that
phrases.meaning: To temporarily set aside a topic for later discussion.
phrases.example: That's an interesting idea, but let's put a pin in that for now.
phrases.plain: That's an interesting idea, but let's save that for later.
phrases.note: Informal but common in American business English for postponing a topic.

phrases.text: Let's put it to a vote
phrases.form: Let's put it to a vote
phrases.meaning: To suggest deciding an issue by having participants formally express their choice.
phrases.example: Since we're divided, let's put it to a vote and move forward.
phrases.plain: Since we're divided, let's vote on it and move forward.
phrases.note: Used when a decision needs to be made and consensus isn't possible.

phrases.meaning: A suggestion to arrange a future conversation to continue a discussion.
phrases.example: We didn't cover everything, so let's schedule another call for next week.
phrases.plain: We didn't cover everything, so we should arrange another call for next week.
phrases.note: Common way to plan continuation of a discussion that couldn't be finished.

phrases.meaning: To remind participants to focus on the planned topics and not digress.
phrases.example: I know that's an interesting point, but let's stick to the agenda for now.
phrases.plain: I know that's an interesting point, but let's keep to the planned topics.
phrases.note: Used by the chair to keep the meeting on track. Can be firm but polite.

phrases.meaning: To postpone discussion of a topic until a later time or meeting.
phrases.example: That's a good point, but let's table that for now and revisit it next week.
phrases.plain: That's a good point, but let's postpone that for now and revisit it next week.
phrases.note: Common in American English for postponing. In British English, 'table' can mean to discuss.

phrases.text: Let's take a quick look at
phrases.form: Let's take a quick look at
phrases.meaning: To suggest a brief review or examination of a topic or document.
phrases.example: Now, let's take a quick look at the revised budget proposal.
phrases.plain: Now, let's briefly review the revised budget proposal.
phrases.note: Common way to introduce a short review. Efficient and direct.

phrases.meaning: To decide on an issue by having participants formally express their choice.
phrases.example: Since we can't reach a consensus, let's take a vote on the final decision.
phrases.plain: Since we can't agree, let's vote on the final decision.
phrases.note: Used when a decision needs to be made and consensus isn't possible.

phrases.meaning: To suggest a short break, usually five minutes, during a long meeting.
phrases.example: We've been going for a while, so let's take five and then resume.
phrases.plain: We've been going for a while, so let's take a short break and then resume.
phrases.note: Informal way to suggest a break. Common in longer meetings.

phrases.meaning: Suggesting a detailed discussion to understand or resolve something.
phrases.example: Let's talk through the options before we make a final decision.
phrases.plain: Let's discuss the options in detail before we decide.
phrases.note: Used to propose a collaborative and thorough discussion.

phrases.meaning: A suggestion to reconnect briefly in the near future to discuss progress or updates.
phrases.example: We've made a plan, so let's touch base soon to review the initial results.
phrases.plain: We've made a plan, so let's talk briefly soon to review the initial results.
phrases.note: Common in professional settings for informal follow-up meetings or calls.

phrases.meaning: A suggestion to bring the current discussion or meeting to a close.
phrases.example: We're almost at time, so let's wrap this up with a summary of decisions.
phrases.plain: We're almost at time, so let's conclude with a summary of decisions.
phrases.note: Informal and direct way to suggest ending a conversation or meeting.

phrases.meaning: to introduce a relatable scenario as an example.
phrases.example: It's hard to manage expectations, like when a client asks for something impossible.
phrases.plain: It's hard to manage expectations, for example when a client asks for something impossible.
phrases.note: Informal, used to provide a common or personal example.

phrases.meaning: the traditional food of a particular region or country.
phrases.example: We're excited to try the local cuisine during our trip to Italy.
phrases.plain: We're excited to try the traditional food of the region during our trip to Italy.
phrases.note: Important aspect of cultural experience.

phrases.meaning: the money used in a particular country.
phrases.example: Do you know where I can exchange my money for local currency?
phrases.plain: Do you know where I can exchange my money for the country's money?
phrases.note: Essential for financial transactions abroad.

phrases.meaning: public transportation within a specific area or city.
phrases.example: The hotel provides excellent information about local transport options.
phrases.plain: The hotel provides excellent information about public transportation within the city.
phrases.note: General term for city-specific transport.

phrases.meaning: A more informal way to summarize a lengthy explanation or narrative quickly.
phrases.example: Long story short, the project was a huge success despite the initial problems.
phrases.plain: To summarize, the project was a huge success despite the initial problems.
phrases.note: A very common, informal way to get to the point quickly. Often used mid-story.

phrases.meaning: An informal greeting used when meeting someone after a long period.
phrases.example: Oh, Sarah! Long time no see, how wonderful to bump into you!
phrases.plain: Oh, Sarah! I haven't seen you in a long time, how wonderful to bump into you!
phrases.note: Very common and friendly, often used as an opening remark.

phrases.meaning: to investigate or examine a problem.
phrases.example: The hotel manager said he would look into it and get back to us.
phrases.plain: The hotel manager said he would investigate the problem and get back to us.
phrases.note: Common response when someone promises to address a problem.

phrases.meaning: To investigate or examine a situation or problem.
phrases.example: I'll look into the matter and get back to you with an update soon.
phrases.plain: I'll investigate the situation and get back to you with an update soon.
phrases.note: A polite and professional way to say you will investigate.

phrases.meaning: Expresses anticipation for a future meeting, call, or interaction.
phrases.example: Thanks for the productive discussion; looking forward to our next meeting.
phrases.plain: Thanks for the productive discussion; I anticipate our next meeting.
phrases.note: Polite and common closing, especially in professional contexts, to maintain rapport.

phrases.meaning: to no longer have one's passport, usually by misplacing it.
phrases.example: I've lost my passport and need to report it to the embassy.
phrases.plain: My passport is missing and I need to report it to the embassy.
phrases.note: Serious travel problem.

phrases.meaning: items that have been lost and found.
phrases.example: I reported my lost wallet at the lost property office at the station.
phrases.plain: I reported my lost wallet at the office for lost and found items.
phrases.note: British English for lost and found.

phrases.meaning: To make a decision, often a difficult or important one.
phrases.example: Someone needs to make a call on whether to proceed with the risky investment.
phrases.plain: Someone needs to decide whether to proceed with the risky investment.
phrases.note: Informal but common for making a judgment.

phrases.meaning: To argue that something is the best thing to do, giving reasons.
phrases.example: The research aims to make a case for increased funding for renewable energy.
phrases.plain: The research aims to argue for increased funding for renewable energy.
phrases.note: Common in persuasive academic writing and policy discussions.

phrases.meaning: To promise to do something or to dedicate oneself to a course of action.
phrases.example: We need them to make a commitment to the long-term maintenance of the system.
phrases.plain: We need them to promise to the long-term maintenance of the system.
phrases.note: Implies a strong promise or dedication.

phrases.meaning: To present a very strong and persuasive reason for something.
phrases.example: She was able to make a compelling argument for increasing the research budget.
phrases.plain: She was able to present a very strong reason for increasing the research budget.
phrases.note: Suggests a highly effective and convincing presentation of ideas.

phrases.meaning: To give up something or agree to something in order to reach an agreement.
phrases.example: We might need to make a concession on the delivery date to secure the deal.
phrases.plain: We might need to compromise on the delivery date to secure the deal.
phrases.note: Formal. Refers to giving ground in a negotiation.

phrases.meaning: To give or provide something, such as ideas, effort, or resources, to a common goal.
phrases.example: I'm eager to make a contribution to your team's success from day one.
phrases.plain: I'm eager to provide something to your team's success from day one.
phrases.note: Shows proactive attitude and team spirit. Very positive in interviews.

phrases.meaning: To respond to an offer with a new offer that proposes different terms.
phrases.example: We'll make a counter-offer that includes a longer payment period.
phrases.plain: We'll respond with a new offer that includes a longer payment period.
phrases.note: Standard negotiation tactic, indicating a willingness to continue discussions.

phrases.meaning: To have a significant positive effect on a situation or person.
phrases.example: I'm motivated by the opportunity to make a difference in people's lives through technology.
phrases.plain: I'm motivated by the opportunity to have a significant positive effect through technology.
phrases.note: Highlights a desire for meaningful work and impact. Very positive.

phrases.meaning: To make a choice or judgment together with others.
phrases.example: We need to make a joint decision on the budget allocation for next year.
phrases.plain: We need to decide together on the budget allocation for next year.
phrases.note: Emphasizes collaborative decision-making.

phrases.meaning: To formally suggest an idea or plan for consideration.
phrases.example: We're ready to make a proposal for the new marketing strategy.
phrases.plain: We're ready to formally suggest an idea for the new marketing strategy.
phrases.note: General term for presenting a plan or suggestion.

phrases.meaning: to book a place or service in advance.
phrases.example: I called the restaurant to make a reservation for two for Friday evening.
phrases.plain: I called the restaurant to book a table for two for Friday evening.
phrases.note: Standard for booking tables, rooms, or tickets.

phrases.meaning: To present a convincing argument or set of reasons for something.
phrases.example: We need to make a strong case for why this project deserves more funding.
phrases.plain: We need to argue convincingly for why this project deserves more funding.
phrases.note: Implies presenting well-reasoned arguments to persuade others.

phrases.meaning: To have a strong effect or influence on something or someone.
phrases.example: I'm looking for a role where I can truly make an impact on the company's growth.
phrases.plain: I'm looking for a role where I can truly have a strong effect on the company's growth.
phrases.note: Highlights a desire for meaningful contribution. Very positive for candidates.

phrases.meaning: To propose a price or terms for a deal.
phrases.example: We're ready to make an offer for the property, but it's below asking price.
phrases.plain: We're ready to propose a price for the property, but it's below asking price.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for presenting a bid or proposal.

phrases.meaning: to ensure something is easily understood and unambiguous.
phrases.example: I want to make it clear that this decision was not taken lightly by the management team.
phrases.plain: I want to state unambiguously that this decision was not taken lightly.
phrases.note: Emphasizes the importance of understanding.

phrases.meaning: to arrive at the scheduled moment.
phrases.example: We left early to make it on time for our train departure.
phrases.plain: We left early to arrive at the scheduled moment for our train departure.
phrases.note: Common for punctuality.

phrases.meaning: To advance or develop in a task or project.
phrases.example: We need to make progress on the new feature development this week.
phrases.plain: We need to advance the new feature development this week.
phrases.note: Used to describe moving forward with a task.

phrases.meaning: To suggest a course of action or advice based on analysis or expertise.
phrases.example: I often had to analyze data and make recommendations to senior management.
phrases.plain: I often had to analyze data and suggest courses of action to senior management.
phrases.note: Highlights analytical and strategic thinking skills. Professional.

phrases.meaning: (as a question) to ask if the explanation is logical.
phrases.example: We'll start with the basics, then move on. Make sense?
phrases.plain: We'll start with the basics, then move on. Is that logical?
phrases.note: Informal, shortened version of "does that make sense."

phrases.meaning: An invitation to a guest to relax and feel comfortable in one's house.
phrases.example: Come in, come in! Make yourself at home, the kitchen is through there.
phrases.plain: Come in, come in! Feel comfortable and relaxed here, the kitchen is through there.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for welcoming guests. Very hospitable.

phrases.meaning: To be responsible for leading and overseeing a group of people.
phrases.example: I have extensive experience in my previous role to manage a team of ten.
phrases.plain: I have extensive experience in my previous role to lead a group of ten.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for leadership and management experience. Very common.

phrases.meaning: To ensure that others have realistic ideas about what is possible or achievable.
phrases.example: It's crucial to manage expectations with stakeholders from the outset of a project.
phrases.plain: It's crucial to ensure stakeholders have realistic ideas from the outset of a project.
phrases.note: Highlights communication and planning skills. Important in project management.

phrases.meaning: To plan, organize, and oversee the execution of specific tasks or initiatives.
phrases.example: I have a proven track record to manage projects from conception to completion.
phrases.plain: I have a proven track record to plan and oversee projects from conception to completion.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for project management experience. Highly valued.

phrases.meaning: A polite and slightly formal request to join the conversation or offer a point.
phrases.example: Excuse me, may I come in here for a moment to share some data?
phrases.plain: Excuse me, may I speak for a moment to share some data?
phrases.note: Polite and slightly more formal than "can I jump in," suitable for meetings.

phrases.meaning: To complete a task or project by the specified time.
phrases.example: I am highly organized and always strive to meet deadlines efficiently.
phrases.plain: I am highly organized and always strive to complete tasks by the specified time.
phrases.note: Highlights reliability and time management skills. Crucial for most roles.

phrases.meaning: To perform as well as or better than what is required or anticipated.
phrases.example: I'm confident in my ability to meet expectations and exceed them in this role.
phrases.plain: I'm confident in my ability to perform as required and exceed it in this role.
phrases.note: Standard phrase for demonstrating capability and commitment to performance.

phrases.meaning: To compromise by each side giving up some demands to reach an agreement.
phrases.example: Perhaps we can meet halfway on the payment schedule to make it work for both.
phrases.plain: Perhaps we can compromise on the payment schedule to make it work for both.
phrases.note: Suggests a willingness to compromise and find a middle ground.

phrases.meaning: bags that have not arrived at the destination with the passenger.
phrases.example: I need to report some missing luggage from my flight from Dublin.
phrases.plain: I need to report that my bags didn't arrive from my flight from Dublin.
phrases.note: Common airport issue.

phrases.meaning: to narrow down a general statement to a particular detail.
phrases.example: We need to improve communication. More specifically, we should implement weekly team check-ins.
phrases.plain: We need to improve communication; we should implement weekly team check-ins.
phrases.note: Used to provide a more focused detail or example.

phrases.meaning: To make progress or continue with a plan or discussion.
phrases.example: We need to agree on these terms to move forward with the project.
phrases.plain: We need to agree on these terms to continue with the project.
phrases.note: Suggests progression and resolution.

phrases.meaning: To proceed with a plan or action.
phrases.example: I suggest we move forward with the proposed changes to the project timeline.
phrases.plain: I suggest we proceed with the proposed changes to the project timeline.
phrases.note: Indicates progression and implementation of a decision.

phrases.meaning: Used to indicate a shift in focus to future actions, plans, or developments.
phrases.example: Moving forward, we plan to implement these changes by the end of the quarter.
phrases.plain: In the future, we plan to implement these changes by the end of the quarter.
phrases.note: Common in business contexts to discuss next steps or future strategy.

phrases.meaning: An advantage or gain that is experienced by all parties involved.
phrases.example: This partnership should be structured for mutual benefit, ensuring success for both companies.
phrases.plain: This partnership should be structured so both companies gain advantages.
phrases.note: Highlights fairness and reciprocal advantages in an agreement.

phrases.meaning: Used to express regret for a mistake or misunderstanding.
phrases.example: My apologies, I seem to have misread that figure on the slide.
phrases.plain: I am sorry, I seem to have misread that figure on the slide.
phrases.note: A polite and formal way to apologize. Can be used for minor errors.

phrases.meaning: Your microphone is turned off, preventing others from hearing you.
phrases.example: Oops, sorry, my audio is muted; I was talking to myself!
phrases.plain: Oops, sorry, my microphone is off; I was talking to myself!
phrases.note: Common self-correction when realizing you've been speaking unheard.

phrases.meaning: Introducing your main worry or problem with a situation.
phrases.example: My concern here is the potential for unforeseen complications with this new software.
phrases.plain: My main worry is the potential for unforeseen complications with this new software.
phrases.note: Clearly states the specific issue that is causing hesitation.

phrases.meaning: The link between your device and the internet, often cited as the cause of call issues.
phrases.example: I apologize, my internet connection seems unstable, which is why my video keeps freezing.
phrases.plain: I apologize, my internet seems unstable, which is why my video keeps freezing.
phrases.note: Used to explain personal technical difficulties. Can be followed by an apology.

phrases.meaning: Used to highlight the most important idea or argument you are presenting.
phrases.example: My main point is that we need to focus on long-term sustainability, not just quick wins.
phrases.plain: The most important idea I want to convey is that we need to focus on long-term sustainability.
phrases.note: Helps to refocus the discussion on the core message.

phrases.meaning: Introduce a single, specific worry or issue you have.
phrases.example: My only concern is that the proposed solution might not be scalable for future growth.
phrases.plain: I am only worried that the proposed solution might not be scalable for future growth.
phrases.note: A polite way to express a reservation, often implying other aspects are fine.

phrases.meaning: Stating your single main concern or doubt about something.
phrases.example: My only reservation is whether we have enough resources to execute this plan effectively.
phrases.plain: My main concern is whether we have enough resources to execute this plan effectively.
phrases.note: Highlights a specific, often crucial, point of hesitation.

phrases.meaning: Offering a personal recommendation for a course of action.
phrases.example: My suggestion would be to hold a brainstorming session next week.
phrases.plain: I suggest we hold a brainstorming session next week.
phrases.note: A polite and slightly formal way to propose an idea.

phrases.meaning: An informal way to say that one is paying for something as a gift.
phrases.example: Let me get this coffee, my treat!
phrases.plain: Let me get this coffee, I am paying for it as a gift!
phrases.note: Friendly and informal, often used for smaller gestures like coffee or a snack.

phrases.meaning: Introduces a statement of what one believes to be true, often for clarification.
phrases.example: My understanding is that the initial quote included all necessary software licenses.
phrases.plain: I believe the initial quote included all necessary software licenses.
phrases.note: Polite way to confirm or clarify information, inviting correction if wrong.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is obvious or expected, but still worth mentioning.
phrases.example: Needless to say, after working all night, I was completely exhausted.
phrases.plain: It's obvious that after working all night, I was completely exhausted.
phrases.note: Emphasizes the obviousness of a consequence or fact.

phrases.meaning: To discuss and agree upon the terms of an arrangement or transaction.
phrases.example: We're working hard to negotiate a deal that benefits both companies.
phrases.plain: We're working hard to discuss and agree upon the terms of an arrangement that benefits both companies.
phrases.note: General term for the process of reaching an agreement.

phrases.meaning: Used to informally introduce the next item on an agenda or the next speaker.
phrases.example: Next up, we have Sarah to talk about the marketing campaign.
phrases.plain: Sarah will speak next about the marketing campaign.
phrases.note: More informal than 'Next, we will look at'. Suitable for team meetings.

phrases.meaning: Expresses strong disbelief or surprise, often informally.
phrases.example: They offered you the job on the spot? No way, that's amazing!
phrases.plain: They offered you the job on the spot? I can't believe it, that's amazing!
phrases.note: A very informal and emphatic expression of disbelief or astonishment.

phrases.meaning: Especially significant or noteworthy among other important things.
phrases.example: The feedback from early adopters is of particular importance to us.
phrases.plain: The feedback from early adopters is especially important to us.
phrases.note: A formal way to highlight something as being more important than others.

phrases.meaning: To suggest a different choice or option.
phrases.example: The study aims to offer an alternative approach to urban development.
phrases.plain: The study aims to suggest a different approach to urban development.
phrases.note: Common in academic proposals when presenting new solutions.

phrases.meaning: To provide a reason or justification for something.
phrases.example: The theory attempts to offer an explanation for the observed phenomena.
phrases.plain: The theory attempts to explain the observed phenomena.
phrases.note: Common in academic writing when presenting theories or interpretations.

phrases.meaning: Expresses exasperation, impatience, or mild annoyance.
phrases.example: Oh, for goodness sake, the printer's jammed again right when I need to print these documents!
phrases.plain: Oh, this is frustrating, the printer's jammed again right when I need to print these documents!
phrases.note: A common exclamation of frustration, often used when something goes wrong repeatedly or unexpectedly.

phrases.meaning: After considering all the relevant factors; generally.
phrases.example: On balance, the benefits of the new system outweigh the initial costs.
phrases.plain: Considering all factors, the benefits of the new system outweigh the initial costs.
phrases.note: Used to give an overall judgment after weighing pros and cons.

phrases.meaning: Referring to the actions or responsibilities of one's own party.
phrases.example: There was a slight delay on our part in sending the revised documents.
phrases.plain: We were slightly delayed in sending the revised documents.
phrases.note: Similar to 'for our part', often used to acknowledge responsibility.

phrases.meaning: Referring to the perspective or position of one's own party.
phrases.example: We have strong arguments on our side regarding the intellectual property.
phrases.plain: We have strong arguments from our perspective regarding the intellectual property.
phrases.note: Indicates one's own position or advantage.

phrases.meaning: happening at the planned time.
phrases.example: Good news, our train is running perfectly on schedule.
phrases.plain: Good news, our train is running exactly at the planned time.
phrases.note: Positive update for travel.

phrases.meaning: Introduces a specific requirement that must be met for something else to happen.
phrases.example: We can agree to that, on the condition that the payment is made upfront.
phrases.plain: We can agree to that, if the payment is made upfront.
phrases.note: Formal way to state a prerequisite for an agreement.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce the first of two contrasting points or arguments.
phrases.example: On the one hand, the results are promising, but further research is needed.
phrases.plain: The results are promising, but further research is needed.
phrases.note: Always followed by 'on the other hand' to present a balanced view.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting point or argument to one previously mentioned.
phrases.example: On the one hand, the costs are high; on the other hand, the potential benefits are immense.
phrases.plain: The costs are high; however, the potential benefits are immense.
phrases.note: Always follows 'on the one hand' to present a balanced view.

phrases.meaning: To have the same understanding or agreement about a situation or plan.
phrases.example: Before we proceed, let's make sure everyone is on the same page regarding the project scope.
phrases.plain: Before we proceed, let's make sure everyone has the same understanding regarding the project scope.
phrases.note: Informal but very common, used to check for alignment.

phrases.meaning: Available for discussion or consideration, usually referring to an offer or proposal.
phrases.example: We have several options on the table for resolving this issue, let's review them.
phrases.plain: We have several options available for resolving this issue, let's review them.
phrases.note: Common in business. Refers to proposals that have been formally presented.

phrases.meaning: Generally; considering everything or everyone.
phrases.example: On the whole, the experiment yielded positive results, though some anomalies occurred.
phrases.plain: Generally, the experiment yielded positive results, though some anomalies occurred.
phrases.note: Similar to 'in general', used for making broad statements.

phrases.meaning: Used to introduce a possible argument or viewpoint, often a cautious one.
phrases.example: One might argue that the benefits outweigh the risks in this particular case.
phrases.plain: The benefits might outweigh the risks in this particular case.
phrases.note: A formal and impersonal way to present a potential argument.

phrases.meaning: Presenting a possible choice or solution among others.
phrases.example: One option would be to reallocate some of the budget to this priority.
phrases.plain: We could reallocate some of the budget to this priority.
phrases.note: A neutral way to introduce a suggestion for consideration.

phrases.meaning: Used to correct or refine a previous statement, offering a more accurate term.
phrases.example: We're targeting a new demographic, or rather, expanding into an adjacent one.
phrases.plain: We're targeting a new demographic, or more accurately, expanding into an adjacent one.
phrases.note: A subtle way to self-correct or clarify a word choice. Very natural.

phrases.meaning: States the absolute minimum or maximum acceptable condition or price.
phrases.example: Our bottom line is that we cannot go below this price point for the service.
phrases.plain: The lowest we can accept is this price point for the service.
phrases.note: Direct and firm. Used to state a non-negotiable limit.

phrases.meaning: not working correctly or broken.
phrases.example: The elevator is out of order, so we'll have to use the stairs.
phrases.plain: The elevator is broken, so we'll have to use the stairs.
phrases.note: Common sign or announcement for broken equipment.

phrases.meaning: to charge someone too much money for something.
phrases.example: I think the taxi driver overcharged me for the ride to the hotel.
phrases.plain: I think the taxi driver charged me too much for the ride to the hotel.
phrases.note: Common complaint about unfair pricing.

phrases.meaning: To successfully deal with difficult situations or problems.
phrases.example: I've learned to overcome challenges by breaking them down into smaller, manageable steps.
phrases.plain: I've learned to deal with difficult situations by breaking them down into smaller steps.
phrases.note: Highlights problem-solving skills and resilience. Excellent for interview answers.

phrases.meaning: the area where passports are checked when entering or leaving a country.
phrases.example: We spent a long time waiting at passport control after our international flight.
phrases.plain: We spent a long time waiting where passports are checked after our international flight.
phrases.note: Essential part of international travel.

phrases.meaning: To make a tentative arrangement or booking.
phrases.example: I'm not 100% sure yet, but you can pencil me in for the barbecue.
phrases.plain: I'm not 100% sure yet, but you can tentatively include me for the barbecue.
phrases.note: Implies a flexible commitment that might change. Informal.

phrases.text: Perhaps we can discuss that offline
phrases.form: Perhaps we can discuss that offline
phrases.meaning: Used to suggest continuing a detailed or specific discussion privately after the presentation.
phrases.example: That's a very specific technical query; perhaps we can discuss that offline.
phrases.plain: That's a very specific technical query; maybe we can talk about it after the presentation.
phrases.note: Useful for managing time or when a question is too niche for the whole audience.

phrases.meaning: Used to make a polite and tentative suggestion for an action.
phrases.example: Perhaps we could try a different approach to engaging with our community.
phrases.plain: Maybe we should try a different approach to engaging with our community.
phrases.note: A diplomatic way to offer an idea, inviting discussion.

phrases.meaning: a designated location where someone or something is collected.
phrases.example: The shuttle bus has a designated pick up point outside the terminal.
phrases.plain: The shuttle bus has a designated place to collect passengers outside the terminal.
phrases.note: Common for tours, taxis, or shuttles.

phrases.meaning: A request on voicemail for the caller to provide comprehensive information.
phrases.example: I'm away from my desk; please leave a detailed message and I'll get back to you.
phrases.plain: I'm away from my desk; please record a comprehensive message and I'll get back to you.
phrases.note: Common on professional voicemail greetings to get necessary information.

phrases.text: point me in the direction of
phrases.form: point me in the direction of
phrases.meaning: to show someone where something is.
phrases.example: Could you please point me in the direction of the nearest ATM?
phrases.plain: Could you please show me where the nearest ATM is?
phrases.note: Polite way to ask for directions.

phrases.meaning: A specific issue or topic about which there is disagreement.
phrases.example: The budget allocation remains a key point of contention among the team members.
phrases.plain: The budget allocation remains a key issue of disagreement among the team members.
phrases.note: Refers to the specific subject of disagreement, often used in formal discussions.

phrases.meaning: To draw attention to a specific fact or detail.
phrases.example: I wanted to point out that the data in section three seems inconsistent with the appendix.
phrases.plain: I wanted to mention that the data in section three seems inconsistent with the appendix.
phrases.note: Used to highlight a specific detail, often a problem or discrepancy.

phrases.meaning: Acknowledge that you understand and accept a criticism or suggestion.
phrases.example: Point taken; I should have communicated the changes more clearly to the whole team.
phrases.plain: I understand your criticism; I should have communicated the changes more clearly.
phrases.note: A concise and direct way to acknowledge and accept a valid point.

phrases.meaning: Expresses sympathy for someone experiencing a minor difficulty or discomfort.
phrases.example: You had to work late again? Poor you, that sounds really exhausting.
phrases.plain: You had to work late again? I feel bad for you, that sounds really exhausting.
phrases.note: A casual, empathetic phrase, often used among friends or close colleagues. Can be slightly teasing if the problem is very minor.

phrases.meaning: Similar to "drop by," to make a quick, informal visit.
phrases.example: I'm just at home, why don't you pop over for a quick chat?
phrases.plain: I'm just at home, why don't you come over quickly for a chat?
phrases.note: Very informal, often implies a short visit. More common in British English.

phrases.meaning: To give reasons and arguments to support a particular point of view.
phrases.example: The speaker will present a case for the ethical use of genetic engineering.
phrases.plain: The speaker will argue for the ethical use of genetic engineering.
phrases.note: Often used in debates, presentations, or persuasive writing.

phrases.meaning: To create a difficult situation or problem that needs to be overcome.
phrases.example: The lack of available data continues to present a challenge for our analysis.
phrases.plain: The lack of available data continues to be a problem for our analysis.
phrases.note: Common in academic discussions when identifying obstacles or difficulties.

phrases.meaning: To offer a set of reasons given with the aim of persuading others that an action or idea is right or wrong.
phrases.example: The paper will present an argument for a revised understanding of the phenomenon.
phrases.plain: The paper will argue for a revised understanding of the phenomenon.
phrases.note: Fundamental in academic writing and debate.

phrases.meaning: To suggest a way to solve a problem.
phrases.example: I'd like to propose a solution that addresses both budget and timeline constraints.
phrases.plain: I'd like to suggest a way to solve the budget and timeline constraints.
phrases.note: Direct and action-oriented, offering a specific remedy.

phrases.meaning: To offer facts, data, or information that supports a claim or argument.
phrases.example: The study aims to provide evidence for the effectiveness of this new teaching method.
phrases.plain: The study aims to show that this new teaching method is effective.
phrases.note: Fundamental in academic and scientific contexts for supporting assertions.

phrases.meaning: To offer constructive criticism or suggestions for improvement.
phrases.example: I believe it's important to provide feedback regularly to team members.
phrases.plain: I believe it's important to offer constructive criticism regularly to team members.
phrases.note: Highlights communication and coaching skills. Professional and positive.

phrases.meaning: To give a clear, deep, and sometimes sudden understanding of a complex matter.
phrases.example: The qualitative data can provide insight into the participants' experiences.
phrases.plain: The qualitative data can help us understand the participants' experiences.
phrases.note: Often used when discussing the value of research findings.

phrases.meaning: To offer help, assistance, or encouragement to someone or something.
phrases.example: I believe it's essential to provide support to new team members during onboarding.
phrases.plain: I believe it's essential to offer help to new team members during onboarding.
phrases.note: Highlights teamwork and mentorship skills. Positive for leadership roles.

phrases.meaning: To set an upper limit on an amount, price, or quantity.
phrases.example: We need to put a cap on the total expenses for this project to stay within budget.
phrases.plain: We need to set an upper limit on the total expenses for this project to stay within budget.
phrases.note: Common in financial or resource-related negotiations.

phrases.meaning: To state a specific amount or price for something.
phrases.example: Can you put a figure on the total cost of the proposed system upgrade?
phrases.plain: Can you state the total cost of the proposed system upgrade?
phrases.note: Commonly used when asking for a price or estimate.
